docs.title: Why does naming matter?
docs.text: Good naming makes code readable, maintainable, and predictable. It reduces cognitive load, helps new team members onboard faster, and prevents bugs caused by misunderstanding what a variable, function, or class is supposed to do. A well-chosen name is the simplest form of documentation.

docs.title: Common
docs.text:
Naming conventions that apply across every language — Python, SQL, JavaScript, Go, or C#. Fix these first before diving into language-specific rules.

General patterns

  • Name for the reader, not the writer. Code is read 10× more than it is written
  • A name should reveal intent without needing a comment: orders_awaiting_shipment not temp2
  • Be precise: customer_email is better than email (which email? the customer's? the sender's?)
  • Be consistent: establish a vocabulary and use it across the entire project
  • Prefer clarity over brevity: delete_expired_sessions() over del_ses()

Useful tips

  • When you struggle to name something, it is often a sign that the design is wrong — simplify first
  • Keep a shared glossary of chosen verbs and nouns for your team or project
  • Read your code aloud — if a name sounds awkward, it probably is
  • Use code review to enforce naming conventions early, before they become habits

docs.title: Abbreviations
docs.text:
General patterns

  • Write names as full words: customer_name not c_nm, user_buffer_size not usr_buf_sz
  • Use standard industry abbreviations only when universally understood: html, url, api, http

Useful tips

  • An abbreviation that saves 3 characters but costs 3 minutes of reader time is a bad trade
  • When in doubt, spell it out — readability beats line length

Abbreviations save typing, but cost readers

bnfd = 12            # What is bnfd? Buffer? Bandwidth? Binary?
dstr = 100.12        # dstr = distance? destination? data stream?
  • Abbreviations that are obvious to you today will be opaque to everyone else tomorrow
  • A name should be understood without consulting a glossary or the author

One-letter names

v = 'comis'          # A string, but what does it represent?
x = calculate()      # What was calculated? Where does x go next?
  • The only acceptable exception is i, j, k as loop counters (and only inside tight loops)
  • Even i should be user_index or page_num when the loop body is longer than 5 lines

docs.title: Consistency
docs.text:
General patterns

  • Pick one verb for each operation and use it everywhere — fetch or get or retrieve, not all three
  • Keep singular/plural distinct: user (one) vs users (many) vs User (class)

Useful tips

  • Inconsistency is worse than a slightly imperfect convention that everyone follows
  • Document your team's vocabulary in a shared glossary

Inconsistent naming across the same codebase

# Three files, three styles for the same operation
get_user()       # file A
fetch_user()     # file B
retrieve_user()  # file C
  • Pick one verb for each operation and use it everywhere: fetch or get or retrieve — not all three
  • Inconsistency is worse than a slightly imperfect convention that everyone follows

Sound-alike names

user    # singular — one user
users   # plural — a collection
User    # class — the blueprint
  • user vs User vs users should never be interchangeable — each has a distinct role
  • Mixing them up in code is a bug waiting to happen

docs.title: Meaning and clarity
docs.text:
General patterns

  • Every name should answer: what is this, and why does it exist here?
  • Use domain vocabulary that matches the problem space

Useful tips

  • If you struggle to name something, simplify the design first
  • A name that needs a comment to explain it is the wrong name

Misleading names

# Name says one thing, code does another
def validate_email(email: str) -> bool:
    return len(email) > 0       # This is not validation
  • A name must reflect what the code actually does, not what you wish it did
  • When the implementation changes, rename the function — don't let the name become a lie

Generic names that convey zero intent

data = fetch()       # What data? From where?
process(data)        # Process how?
tmp = transform(x)   # Temp for what?
  • data, info, tmp, thing, obj, item, stuff — these names say nothing
  • Every name should answer: what is this, and why does it exist here?

Names that fight the domain

# In a finance or e-commerce system
temp = get_balance(account_id)   # temp suggests it's throwaway — it isn't
x = apply_discount(code, total)  # x is a discounted total, not a coordinate
  • Use domain vocabulary: a payment has a status, not a flag. A customer has an email, not a contact_string
  • Names that ignore the domain force the next reader to translate back and forth

docs.title: Verbs
docs.text: A curated reference of action verbs for naming functions, methods, and operations. Pick a verb and pair it with a domain noun — add_order(), validate_email(), to_json(), from_row().

docs.title: A
docs.text: Verb Meaning Example name accept Take or receive something offered accept_invitation() access Gain entry to or use of something access_database() acquire Obtain something, especially after an effort acquire_lock() activate Make something active or operational activate_account() add Bring together or unite to increase the number, quantity, or importance add_item() adjust Alter or move something slightly to achieve the desired fit or result adjust_brightness() aggregate Collect into a mass or whole aggregate_sales() alert Warn or notify about a problem or danger alert_admin() align Place or arrange things in a straight line or in a proper position align_text() allocate Distribute or assign for a particular purpose allocate_resources() analyze Examine methodically and in detail the constitution or structure of analyze_pattern() append Add something to the end of a document or piece of data append_data() apply Put into operation or effect apply_discount() archive Move data to long-term storage archive_records() arrange Organize or put in order arrange_columns() assign Allocate or distribute a task or responsibility assign_task() associate Connect someone or something with something else in memory or imagination associate_tag() attach Fasten, join, or connect something to something else attach_file() attempt Make an effort to achieve or complete something authenticate_user() audit Conduct a systematic examination of books, accounts, or records audit_log() authenticate Verify the identity of a user or system authenticate_request() authorize Give official permission or approval to authorize_payment() average Calculate the mean value of a set of numbers average_score()

docs.title: B
docs.text: Verb Meaning Example name backup Create a duplicate copy for safety or recovery backup_database() balance Make or keep things in a steady state balance_load() batch Process multiple items as a single group batch_insert() bind Tie together or hold together bind_values() block Prevent something from happening or progressing block_user() bootstrap Start a system or process that initializes other parts bootstrap_app() borrow Take and use something with the intention of returning it borrow_resource() branch Split into different directions or paths branch_logic() broadcast Send out a message or signal to multiple recipients broadcast_event() browse Look through or examine something casually browse_directory() buffer Temporarily store data to balance processing rates buffer_stream() build Construct or create something by putting parts together build_query() bundle Combine items into a single package or unit bundle_products() burn Process or destroy data intentionally burn_image() bypass Go around or avoid a particular step or obstacle bypass_cache()

docs.title: C
docs.text: Verb Meaning Example name cache Store duplicate copies of data for faster access cache_response() calculate Determine a result by mathematical or logical means calculate_total() cancel Decide or announce that an arranged event will not take place cancel_order() capture Take into one's possession or control capture_output() cast Convert one data type to another cast_to_int() catch Intercept and handle an exception or error catch_exception() check Examine or test something to ensure it meets requirements check_status() clean Remove unwanted elements or make something orderly clean_data() clear Make something empty or free from obstruction clear_cache() clone Make an exact copy of something clone_repository() close Shut down or end a connection or process close_connection() collect Gather or bring together things from different sources collect_feedback() combine Join or mix together to form a single entity combine_datasets() commit Save changes permanently to a repository or database commit_transaction() compare Examine the similarities and differences between compare_versions() compile Translate source code into machine code or an executable compile_code() complete Bring to an end or fulfill all requirements complete_task() compose Create something by combining different parts compose_message() compute Calculate or determine something mathematically compute_average() configure Set up or arrange the parts of a system or process configure_system() connect Join or establish a relationship or communication link connect_database() consume Use up or absorb resources or data consume_api() convert Change from one form, purpose, or use to another convert_currency() copy Create a duplicate of something copy_file() count Determine the number of elements in a collection count_items() create Bring something into existence or make something new create_user()

docs.text: Meaning: A money amount in the smallest currency unit Example: price_cents, refund_cents, fee_cents Avoid: Float amounts such as price with no unit

docs.title: _code
docs.text: Meaning: A short coded value from a fixed set Example: country_code, error_code, currency_code Avoid: type when the value is a code

docs.title: _count
docs.text: Meaning: The number of items in a collection Example: item_count, error_count, retry_count Avoid: Using number or total when referring to a count

docs.title: _date
docs.text: Meaning: A calendar date without time component Example: birth_date, order_date, expiry_date Avoid: day which is ambiguous (could mean day of month or calendar day)

docs.title: _days
docs.text: Meaning: A duration in days Example: retention_days, trial_days, grace_days Avoid: duration or period with no unit

docs.title: _hash
docs.text: Meaning: A digest of other data Example: password_hash, content_hash, commit_hash Avoid: checksum unless it is a real checksum

docs.title: _hours
docs.text: Meaning: A duration in hours Example: valid_hours, ttl_hours, sla_hours Avoid: hours alone for a duration

docs.title: _id
docs.text: Meaning: Identifier for a specific entity Example: user_id, order_id, session_id Avoid: Bare id when there might be ambiguity about what is being identified

docs.title: _ids
docs.text: Meaning: A collection of identifiers Example: order_ids, user_ids, parent_ids Avoid: id_list which repeats _list

docs.title: _index
docs.text: Meaning: Position in an ordered sequence Example: page_index, record_index, current_index Avoid: position which is longer and less precise

docs.title: _key
docs.text: Meaning: A value that identifies or looks up an item Example: api_key, cache_key, partition_key Avoid: id when the value is a lookup key

docs.title: _limit
docs.text: Meaning: A maximum that the system enforces Example: rate_limit, size_limit, retry_limit Avoid: max when the system rejects values above it

docs.title: _list
docs.text: Meaning: A collection or array of items Example: product_list, error_list, pending_tasks Avoid: array which is implementation-specific

docs.title: _map
docs.text: Meaning: A key-value data structure Example: user_map, settings_map, cache_map Avoid: dictionary or hash which are language-specific terms

docs.title: _max
docs.text: Meaning: The highest allowed or observed value Example: retry_max, price_max, length_max Avoid: high or top

docs.title: _min
docs.text: Meaning: The lowest allowed or observed value Example: price_min, length_min, age_min Avoid: low or bottom

docs.title: _minutes
docs.text: Meaning: A duration in minutes Example: timeout_minutes, lock_minutes, delay_minutes Avoid: mins or bare minutes

docs.title: _ms
docs.text: Meaning: A duration in milliseconds Example: latency_ms, timeout_ms, elapsed_ms Avoid: time or delay with no unit

docs.title: _name
docs.text: Meaning: A human-readable label Example: first_name, file_name, team_name Avoid: title or label for the same meaning in one codebase

docs.title: _path
docs.text: Meaning: A location in a file system or tree Example: config_path, output_path, json_path Avoid: url when the value is not a URL

docs.title: _percent
docs.text: Meaning: A value from 0 to 100 Example: discount_percent, cpu_percent, fill_percent Avoid: rate or pct when the scale is unclear

docs.title: _rate
docs.text: Meaning: A quantity per unit of time or per base amount Example: error_rate, tax_rate, sample_rate Avoid: ratio when the value is a rate

docs.title: _ratio
docs.text: Meaning: A value from 0 to 1 that compares two quantities Example: hit_ratio, discount_ratio, fail_ratio Avoid: percent when the scale is 0 to 1

docs.title: _seconds
docs.text: Meaning: A duration in seconds Example: timeout_seconds, ttl_seconds, interval_seconds Avoid: timeout alone, which hides the unit

docs.title: _size
docs.text: Meaning: The number of elements or the capacity Example: page_size, batch_size, pool_size Avoid: length or count when it means capacity

docs.title: _status
docs.text: Meaning: The current state of a process or entity Example: payment_status, order_status, sync_status Avoid: state and status mixed in one codebase

docs.title: _total
docs.text: Meaning: The sum of all values in a collection Example: order_total, price_total, amount_total Avoid: Using bare total without specifying what is being totaled

docs.title: _type
docs.text: Meaning: The kind of an item from a fixed set Example: event_type, account_type, media_type Avoid: kind and type mixed in one codebase

docs.title: _url
docs.text: Meaning: A uniform resource locator Example: api_url, base_url, endpoint_url Avoid: link or address which are less specific

docs.title: _uuid
docs.text: Meaning: A universally unique identifier Example: request_uuid, session_uuid, trace_uuid Avoid: _id when the format is a UUID and the format matters

docs.title: _version
docs.text: Meaning: A numbered revision Example: schema_version, api_version, app_version Avoid: rev or ver

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
General patterns

  • Use the type system and annotations to convey type information — not the name
  • Names should describe purpose, not implementation

Useful tips

  • Language-ambiguous contexts (older JavaScript, PHP, Bash) may still benefit from type prefixes — evaluate per-language

Names that include type information (Hungarian)

strName = "Alice"         # The annotation tells us it's a string
intCount = 5              # Python 3+ has type hints
dictUsers = {}            # The {} literal already signals a dict
  • Type information in the name is noise — type annotations and IDEs handle this
  • Exception: type-ambiguous languages without type hints (JavaScript, etc.)

Redundant prefixes

my_variable = ...         # Whose else would it be?
the_value = ...           # Which other value?
local_counter = ...       # It's already local by scope
  • my_, the_, local_ — strip these prefixes. They add length and add nothing

docs.title: Databases
docs.text:
General naming conventions for database schemas — tables, columns, indexes, constraints, and relationships.

General patterns

  • Use snake_case for all database identifiers
  • Be consistent: the same concept should have the same name across every table
  • Use descriptive names that reflect the business domain
  • Explicitly name every constraint — auto-generated names are unreadable in error logs

Useful tips

  • Design the schema before writing migrations — naming decisions affect every query
  • Keep a data dictionary for your team to align on column meanings
  • Prefer singular names for lookup tables and plural for data tables

  • Tables

    Plural nouns, junction tables, lookup tables — schema-level naming.

    Tables

  • Columns

    Foreign keys, booleans, timestamps, counters, monetary values — column-level conventions.

    Columns

  • Indexes

    idx_ and uq_ prefixes, index kinds, column order in composite indexes.

    Indexes

  • Constraints

    Primary keys, foreign keys, check constraints — pk_, fk_, chk_ naming.

    Constraints

  • Enumerated columns

    Database enums, lookup tables, CHECK constraints — when to use what.

    Enums

  • Warehouse and analytics

    dbt layers, medallion layers, fact and dimension tables, keys, SCD type 2.

    Warehouse

docs.title: E-commerce schema
docs.text:
Table Columns Notes users id, email, first_name, last_name, is_active, created_at Plural, natural PK on email orders id, user_id, status, total_cents, currency, shipped_at, created_at total_cents = int, avoids float rounding order_items id, order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price_cents Junction table products id, sku, name, price_cents, is_available, stock_count sku = natural secondary key shipping_addresses id, user_id, street, city, country_code, is_default One user can have many addresses

See also

  • Naming patterns for rules about booleans, units and time
  • Languages for the case style in the code that reads these tables
  • REST and Events for the same names in an API and in messages
  • Examples for complete schemas in seven domains

docs.title: Columns
docs.text:
General patterns

  • Use snake_case: first_name, created_at, order_total
  • Primary key: id (surrogate) or a descriptive natural key: email, slug. Warehouse tables use _key for surrogate keys (see Warehouse)
  • Foreign key: <referenced_table_singular>_id: user_id, order_id, country_code
  • Boolean columns: is_ or has_ prefix: is_active, has_shipped, is_available
  • Timestamps: _at suffix: created_at, updated_at, deleted_at, expires_at
  • Dates: _date suffix: start_date, end_date, birth_date
  • Counters: _count suffix: login_count, retry_count, item_count
  • Monetary values: include currency or unit: amount_cents, price_cents with currency_code, balance_btc

Useful tips

  • Don't repeat the table name in a column name: users.name not users.user_name
  • Use the same column name across tables for the same concept: created_at everywhere, not created in one table and created_at in another
  • Name soft-delete columns consistently: deleted_at (nullable timestamp) is clearer than a boolean is_deleted for point-in-time recovery
  • For polymorphic foreign keys, use <target>_type and <target>_id: document_type, document_id

General anti-patterns

  • Hungarian prefixes: vc_name, i_id, dt_created — type info belongs in the schema, not the name
  • Abbreviations that save only 1-2 characters: cust_addr → customer_address, qty → quantity
  • Generic names like value, code, type, desc in tables where they could mean anything
  • Using reserved words: order, group, select, from, table — wrap in quotes everywhere or just rename

docs.title: Examples by kind
docs.text: The tables use an e-commerce checkout. The patterns follow Booleans, collections, units and time. In SQL, all names use snake_case.

docs.title: Audit columns
docs.text: Column Type idea Meaning Why this name created_at timestamp with time zone When the row was inserted. _at marks a moment. updated_at timestamp with time zone When the row last changed. Same suffix as created_at. deleted_at timestamp with time zone, nullable When the row was soft-deleted. NULL means live. A timestamp says when. A boolean does not. created_by_user_id foreign key to users Who created the row. A role plus the table: <role>_<table_singular>_id. updated_by_user_id foreign key to users Who changed the row last. Same pattern. row_version integer A counter for optimistic locking. version alone could mean a product version. source_system text Where the row came from. Names the origin, not the type.

docs.title: Money and currency
docs.text:
Store money as an integer in minor units plus a currency code. For other approaches, see Booleans, collections, units and time.

Column Type idea Meaning Why this name total_amount_cents bigint The order total in cents. The unit is in the name. Inside orders, drop the order_ prefix. tax_amount_cents bigint The tax part of the total. Same unit as the total. discount_amount_cents bigint The discount in cents. discount alone could be a rate. currency_code char(3) The ISO 4217 code, such as EUR. code states the format. unit_price_minor_units bigint The price in minor units for currencies that do not use cents. _minor_units replaces _cents for other currencies. eur_to_usd_rate numeric The rate from euro to US dollar. Name the direction of the rate. discount_rate numeric The discount as a ratio from 0 to 1. rate marks a ratio.

docs.title: Temporal columns
docs.text: Column Type idea Meaning Why this name starts_at timestamp with time zone When an offer begins. A matching pair with ends_at. ends_at timestamp with time zone When an offer ends. Same suffix. valid_from timestamp with time zone Start of a validity period. A pair with valid_to. A common exception to the _at rule. valid_to timestamp with time zone, nullable End of a validity period. NULL means open. Document whether the end is included. birth_date date A calendar date. _date marks a date with no time. delivery_date date The planned delivery day. Same suffix. expires_at timestamp with time zone, nullable When a token stops working. NULL can mean it never expires. last_login_at timestamp with time zone, nullable The last login moment. last_ plus a timestamp name.

docs.title: JSON and array columns
docs.text:
The type ideas use PostgreSQL names. The column names apply to any JSON type. MySQL has JSON and no array type. SQL Server stores JSON as text, or in a native json type on newer versions, and has no array type.

Column Type idea Meaning Why this name raw_payload jsonb The original webhook body. Names the content, not the type. shipping_options jsonb A bag of options for shipping. A plural noun for a group. attributes jsonb Flexible product attributes. The content word, not data. settings jsonb Per-account settings. A common noun for configuration. tags text array The labels of a product. A plural noun for an array. allowed_country_codes text array The countries where an offer runs. Array elements cannot have a foreign key. Plural and states the format.

Do not put the type in the name: tags_array and settings_json repeat what the schema says. Use an array only for a small list that you never join. For anything else, use a junction table (see Tables).

docs.title: Tenant, polymorphic and enum columns
docs.text:
Column Type idea Meaning Why this name tenant_id foreign key The customer account that owns the row. The same name in every table. organization_id foreign key The company that owns the row. <table_singular>_id pattern. owner_type text The kind of record that owns this row, such as order. <target>_type pairs with <target>_id. owner_id bigint The id of the owning record. Pairs with owner_type. commentable_type text The kind of record that has the comment. A role word ending in able is common in Rails. commentable_id bigint The id of that record. Pairs with commentable_type. status enum or text The state of the order. Do not repeat the table name: orders.status. payment_method enum or text How the customer pays. A noun for the choice. shipping_carrier enum or text The carrier that delivers. A noun for the choice.

A polymorphic _id cannot have a foreign key constraint. Prefer one nullable foreign key per target when the set of targets is small. For enum types and their values, see Enums.

docs.title: Booleans, counters and units
docs.text: Column Type idea Meaning Why this name is_active boolean The row is in use. The positive form. has_gift_wrap boolean The order has gift wrap. has_ marks ownership. item_count integer The number of items in the cart. _count marks a counter. retry_count integer The number of retries. Same suffix. package_weight_grams integer The weight in grams. The unit is in the name. file_size_bytes bigint The size of a file. The unit is in the name. timeout_seconds integer A timeout in seconds. No guess about seconds or milliseconds. distance_km numeric A distance in kilometres. A standard unit symbol.

docs.title: Identifier limits and case
docs.text:
Database Maximum length of a name Case rule Note PostgreSQL 63 bytes Folds unquoted names to lower case. A longer name is cut to 63 bytes, with a notice. A quoted mixed-case name needs quotes in every query. MySQL 64 characters for most names Column names are not case-sensitive. Table names can be, depending on the system. Check lower_case_table_names. SQL Server 128 characters Depends on the collation. The same name can differ by case in one database and not in another.

Use short, lower-case names without quotes. Then the same name works in every database. See PostgreSQL lexical structure, MySQL identifiers and SQL Server database identifiers.

docs.title: Bad → better
docs.text:
Bad Better Why OrderID order_id PostgreSQL folds an unquoted OrderID to orderid. A quoted "OrderID" needs quotes in every query. is_deleted deleted_at A timestamp says when. NULL means not deleted. price FLOAT price_cents BIGINT plus currency_code Integer minor units avoid rounding errors. amount total_amount_cents A bare amount hides the unit. created created_at _at marks a timestamp. date delivery_date date is a type name and a vague word. status_ok is_status_ok A boolean reads as a statement. weight package_weight_grams The unit is in the name. data_json raw_payload Name the content, not the type. tags_array tags The schema already shows the array type. fk_user user_id A foreign key column is <referenced_table_singular>_id. type payment_method type alone could mean anything. qty quantity Saves two letters and costs clarity. order (as a column) order_number order is a reserved word. tenant tenant_id A foreign key ends with _id, or with the referenced natural key, such as country_code.

See also

  • Tables, Indexes, Constraints and Enums
  • Negation and optionality for NULL and missing values
  • Bad → better cookbook for more rewrites

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
General patterns

  • Primary key: pk_<table> — pk_customers, pk_order_items
  • Foreign key: fk_<table>_<referenced_table> — fk_orders_customers, fk_order_items_orders
  • Check constraint: chk_<table>_<description> — chk_orders_total_amount_cents_non_negative, chk_customers_age_range
  • Unique constraint: uq_<table>_<columns>, the same as for unique indexes — uq_customers_email

Useful tips

  • Explicitly name constraints rather than relying on auto-generated names — error messages become readable: "violates fk_orders_customers" tells you exactly which key failed
  • For composite foreign keys, use the same pattern. The definition lists the columns: fk_order_items_product_variants

General anti-patterns

  • Auto-generated constraint names like FK__orders__customer_id__5A3B6F — unreadable in error logs
  • Skipping foreign key constraints entirely — data integrity should be enforced at the database level, not just in the application
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT pk_orders PRIMARY KEY (id);
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT fk_orders_customers FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(id);
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT chk_orders_total_amount_cents_non_negative CHECK (total_amount_cents >= 0);

docs.title: Constraint kinds
docs.text:
The examples use an e-commerce checkout. All names have the form <prefix>_<table>_<description>, except pk_<table>.

Kind Pattern Example Why this name Primary key pk_<table> pk_orders A table has one primary key. The table name is enough. Composite primary key pk_<table> pk_user_roles Same pattern. List the columns in the definition, not in the name. Foreign key fk_<table>_<referenced_table> fk_orders_customers Child table first, then the parent. Foreign key, second link to a table fk_<table>_<role> fk_orders_billing_address, fk_orders_shipping_address When a table has two keys to one parent, name the role. Foreign key on a junction fk_<table>_<referenced_table> fk_user_roles_roles Same pattern. Foreign key, composite fk_<table>_<referenced_table> fk_order_items_product_variants The name stays short. The definition lists the columns. Unique uq_<table>_<columns> uq_products_sku The same prefix as a unique index. Unique composite uq_<table>_<col1>_<col2> uq_coupon_redemptions_coupon_id_customer_id A customer uses a coupon once. Check, range chk_<table>_<description> chk_orders_discount_rate_range The description states the rule. Check, sign chk_<table>_<column>_<rule> chk_orders_total_amount_cents_non_negative The column and the rule. Check, positive chk_<table>_<column>_positive chk_order_items_quantity_positive A common rule has a fixed word. Check, order of dates chk_<table>_<later>_after_<earlier> chk_shipments_delivered_after_shipped The words state the order. Check, pair chk_<table>_<a>_after_<b> chk_coupons_ends_after_starts Matches the starts_at and ends_at pair. Check, allowed values chk_<table>_<column>_allowed chk_payments_method_allowed Use a lookup table when the list changes often. A PostgreSQL enum cannot drop a value. Check, format chk_<table>_<column>_format chk_currency_code_format For example code ~ '^[A-Z]{3}$'. Exclusion ex_<table>_<description> ex_price_rules_no_overlap PostgreSQL only. The period of two rows must not overlap. Default (SQL Server) df_<table>_<column> df_orders_status Only SQL Server names a default as an object.

docs.title: More examples
docs.text: Constraint Kind pk_customers, pk_order_items, pk_products Primary key fk_order_items_orders, fk_order_items_products, fk_payments_orders Foreign key uq_customers_email, uq_shipping_carrier_code Unique chk_products_weight_grams_positive, chk_customers_age_range Check

docs.title: Not null
docs.text: Most databases do not let you name a NOT NULL rule. Do not try. Put the rule in the column definition and read it in the schema. Oracle and PostgreSQL 18 and newer can store a name for it. This is rarely worth the work.

docs.title: Auto-generated names
docs.text:
Always name constraints yourself. The default names differ by database and are hard to read in an error.

Database Default names Example PostgreSQL <table>_pkey, <table>_<column>_fkey, <table>_<column>_key, <table>_<column>_check orders_customer_id_fkey MySQL PRIMARY, <table>_ibfk_<n>, <table>_chk_<n> orders_ibfk_1 SQL Server PK__<table>__<hash>, FK__<table>__<column>__<hash> FK__orders__user_id__5A3B6F

Names with a counter or a hash change when you create the schema again. A migration that drops a constraint by its default name can fail on another server. See the PostgreSQL pages on constraints and the MySQL page on FOREIGN KEY constraints.

docs.title: Scope of constraint names
docs.text:
Database Where the name must be unique PostgreSQL In the table. A key that has an index also needs a free name in the schema, because the index takes the same name. MySQL Foreign key and check names: in the database. Unique names are index names: in the table. A primary key is always PRIMARY, whatever name you give. SQL Server In the schema.

Put the table name in every constraint name. Then the same name works in all three databases.

docs.title: Examples in SQL
docs.text:
ALTER TABLE order_items ADD CONSTRAINT pk_order_items PRIMARY KEY (order_id, line_number);
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT fk_orders_billing_address FOREIGN KEY (billing_address_id) REFERENCES addresses (id);
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT fk_orders_shipping_address FOREIGN KEY (shipping_address_id) REFERENCES addresses (id);
ALTER TABLE coupons ADD CONSTRAINT chk_coupons_ends_after_starts CHECK (ends_at > starts_at);
ALTER TABLE coupon_redemptions ADD CONSTRAINT uq_coupon_redemptions_coupon_id_customer_id UNIQUE (coupon_id, customer_id);
ALTER TABLE price_rules ADD CONSTRAINT ex_price_rules_no_overlap
    EXCLUDE USING gist (product_id WITH =, validity WITH &&);

The exclusion example needs the btree_gist extension and a range column named validity.

docs.title: Bad → better
docs.text:
Bad Better Why FK__orders__user_id__5A3B6F fk_orders_customers The default name has a hash. fk1 fk_orders_customers A number says nothing. orders_ibfk_1 fk_orders_customers A counter changes when you create the schema again. check_1 chk_orders_total_amount_cents_non_negative The name states the rule. chk_orders_valid chk_orders_discount_rate_range valid says nothing. fk_orders_addresses twice, when orders has two links to addresses fk_orders_billing_address and fk_orders_shipping_address Two keys to one parent need a role. uq_email uq_customers_email The name lacks the table. pk pk_orders The name lacks the table. chk_age chk_customers_age_range Name the table and the rule. ck_status_in_list for a list that changes each month a lookup table plus fk_orders_order_status A check cannot change without a migration.

See also

  • Indexes for uq_ indexes and the same naming rules
  • Tables and Columns for the names that go into constraint names
  • Enums for a list of allowed values

docs.title: Enums
docs.text:
General patterns

  • Use database-native ENUM or CREATE TYPE when the set of values is stable and small
  • Use a lookup table when the set may grow or needs metadata (display names, sort order)
  • Use CHECK constraints when enum type is not available in the database

Prefer lookup tables over hard-coded enums when the values are business concepts: order_status, shipping_method, payment_provider

  • Business enums change more often than code enums — a lookup table lets you add values without a migration

docs.title: Indexes
docs.text:
General patterns

  • Use idx_<table>_<columns> for regular indexes: idx_customers_email, idx_orders_customer_id_created_at
  • Use uq_<table>_<columns> for unique indexes: uq_customers_email, uq_country_code
  • Write the columns in the name in the same order as in the index. Choose that order for the queries (see "Column order in an index name")

Useful tips

  • Name composite indexes after the columns in the order they appear in the index: idx_orders_customer_id_created_at
  • Drop unused indexes — every index adds write overhead

General anti-patterns

  • Index names without the table name: idx_1, ix_email (which table?)
  • Generic suffixes like _idx without the table context
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_id ON orders(customer_id);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_customers_email ON customers(email);
CREATE INDEX idx_order_items_order_id_product_id ON order_items(order_id, product_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_id_created_at_desc ON orders(customer_id, created_at DESC);

docs.title: Index kinds
docs.text:
The examples use an e-commerce checkout. Add a suffix for the index method only when the method is not B-tree. B-tree is the default, so most names have no suffix.

Kind Pattern Example Why this name Single column idx_<table>_<column> idx_orders_customer_id The table and the column, in this order. Foreign key support idx_<table>_<fk_column> idx_order_items_order_id Same pattern. A foreign key needs an index on the child side for fast joins and deletes. PostgreSQL does not make it for you. MySQL InnoDB makes one and names it after the constraint. Composite idx_<table>_<col1>_<col2> idx_orders_customer_id_created_at Column order in the name equals column order in the index. Descending idx_<table>_<columns>_desc idx_orders_customer_id_created_at_desc Add _desc only for a mixed sort, such as customer_id ASC, created_at DESC. A single-column B-tree index can be read backward. Unique uq_<table>_<columns> uq_customers_email uq_ marks a rule, not only speed. Unique composite uq_<table>_<col1>_<col2> uq_order_items_order_id_product_id One product only once per order. Partial idx_<table>_<columns>_<condition> idx_orders_created_at_open The condition word says which rows are in the index. Partial unique uq_<table>_<columns>_<condition> uq_customers_email_not_deleted Unique only for rows where deleted_at IS NULL. Covering idx_<table>_<columns>_incl_<columns> idx_orders_customer_id_incl_total_cents incl is short for INCLUDE. This is a convention of this guide. Expression idx_<table>_<function>_<column> idx_customers_lower_email The function is part of what you search for. Unique expression uq_<table>_<function>_<column> uq_customers_lower_email A case-insensitive unique email. GIN idx_<table>_<column>_gin idx_products_attributes_gin For jsonb, arrays and full-text search. GIN for text search idx_<table>_<column>_gin idx_products_search_vector_gin The column holds a tsvector. GIN for trigrams idx_<table>_<column>_trgm idx_customers_last_name_trgm pg_trgm serves LIKE '%text%'. GiST idx_<table>_<column>_gist idx_shipping_zones_area_gist For geometry and ranges. BRIN idx_<table>_<column>_brin idx_events_created_at_brin A small index for a big table that is stored in order. Hash idx_<table>_<column>_hash idx_sessions_token_hash Equality lookups only. Do not confuse it with a column named token_hash.

The method names (gin, gist, brin, hash) are PostgreSQL. Other databases use other kinds. For example, MySQL has FULLTEXT and SPATIAL indexes.

docs.text: Index Kind idx_payments_order_id, idx_shipments_order_id, idx_products_category_id Foreign key support idx_coupon_redemptions_customer_id, idx_orders_status_created_at Single and composite idx_webhook_deliveries_event_id_created_at Composite uq_products_sku, uq_coupons_code Unique

docs.title: Column order in an index name
docs.text:
Write the columns in the same order as in the index. Choose that order for the queries, not for the name:

  1. Put columns that you compare with = first.
  2. Put the column with a range (>, BETWEEN) or a sort after them.
  3. Put a column in the index only if a query uses it.

For example, the query WHERE customer_id = ? AND created_at > ? needs idx_orders_customer_id_created_at. The reverse order would scan more entries. A B-tree index helps a query most when the query uses its leftmost columns. See the PostgreSQL pages on multicolumn indexes, partial indexes and index types.

docs.title: Name length and scope
docs.text:
Database Index name scope Limit PostgreSQL Unique in the schema. 63 bytes. A longer name is cut. MySQL Unique per table. 64 characters. SQL Server Unique per table. 128 characters.

The table name in the index name keeps names unique in PostgreSQL and clear in every database. If a name is too long, shorten the column words in the same way everywhere, for example cust_id. Keep names under 63 bytes. PostgreSQL cuts a longer name, two cut names can become equal, and then the second CREATE fails.

PostgreSQL makes a name when you give none: <table>_<column>_idx. This is a valid but weak choice, because it lacks a prefix that tells unique from non-unique.

docs.title: Bad → better
docs.text:
Bad Better Why idx_1 idx_orders_customer_id A number says nothing. ix_email idx_customers_email The name lacks the table. email_idx idx_customers_email The name lacks the table. Use the prefix form. idx_orders_created_at_customer_id for WHERE customer_id = ? ORDER BY created_at idx_orders_customer_id_created_at The equality column goes first. idx_customers_email (case-insensitive search by lower(email)) idx_customers_lower_email The name must match what the index stores. idx_orders_status on a column with 3 values a partial index such as idx_orders_created_at_open A low-selectivity index on its own rarely helps. idx_orders_all idx_orders_customer_id_created_at all is not a column. index_new, idx_test name the real columns Never commit these. idx_order_items_order_id_product_id_quantity_unit_price_cents_created_at idx_order_items_order_id_product_id Too long. Keep the columns that the queries need. idx_customers_email for a unique rule uq_customers_email A rule that blocks duplicates needs the uq_ prefix.

See also

  • Constraints for the rules that create unique indexes
  • Tables and Columns for the names that go into index names
  • Bad → better cookbook for more rewrites

docs.title: Tables
docs.text:
General patterns

  • Use snake_case and plural nouns: users, orders, order_items, shipping_addresses
  • Use singular nouns for lookup / enum tables: country, currency, order_status
  • Junction (many-to-many) tables: combine both entity names, listing the primary/owner entity first: user_roles, product_categories, student_courses
  • Junction table PK: for a pure link table, use a composite key (a_id, b_id), not a surrogate id. If the same pair can repeat, such as two redemptions of one coupon, use a surrogate id
  • Use a single-word name when possible; two words if needed: invoices not customer_invoice_data

Useful tips

  • Avoid prefixes and suffixes: users not tbl_users or users_table
  • Keep table names under 30 characters for cross-database portability
  • Use consistent singular/plural — plural for rows (collections), singular for dictionaries (status, type)

General anti-patterns

  • Prefixes like tbl_, tab_, tb_ — they add noise and serve no purpose
  • Names like Table1, tmp, test — never commit these
  • Including the database or schema name in the table name: app_users inside the app schema

docs.title: Singular or plural?
docs.text:
Both styles work. Choose one style and use it for all tables of the same kind.

Style Examples Who uses it Why choose it Plural for entity tables users, orders, order_items Rails: Active Record basics names tables in the plural A table holds many rows. Queries read well: FROM orders. Singular for lookup tables country, currency, order_status This guide A lookup table is a dictionary of values. Singular for all tables user, order, order_item Some teams The table name matches the model name. order and user are reserved words in PostgreSQL, so they need quotes. App prefix plus model name shop_order, shop_orderitem Django: see model options for db_table The default is the app label, an underscore and the lower-case model name, with no underscores inside it. Set db_table to get other names.

This guide uses plural names for entity tables and singular names for lookup tables. A container noun stays singular: audit_log, job_queue, order_history, order_archive.

docs.title: Examples by kind
docs.text: The tables use an e-commerce checkout. For column names inside these tables, see Columns.

docs.title: Entity and junction tables
docs.text:
Table Kind Meaning Why this name customers Entity The people who buy. A plural noun. orders Entity The purchases. A plural noun. order_items Dependent entity The lines of an order. The owner first, then the part. shipping_addresses Entity Addresses for delivery. A plural noun with a clear role. product_categories Junction Links products to categories. Both entity names. customer_roles Junction Links customers to roles. The owner first. coupon_redemptions Junction with data A customer used a coupon. A domain word for a link with its own attributes. enrollments Junction with data A student takes a course. Name the meaning, not both table names.

A junction table with extra data usually has its own domain name. order_items carries quantity and price, so it is not named order_products.

docs.title: Lookup tables
docs.text:
Table Meaning Why this name country ISO countries. A dictionary, singular. currency ISO 4217 currencies. A dictionary, singular. order_status Allowed order states. A dictionary, singular. payment_method Allowed ways to pay. A dictionary, singular. shipping_carrier Known carriers. A dictionary, singular.

For enum types and their values, see Enums.

Name clash in PostgreSQL

PostgreSQL makes a row type with the name of each table. A table order_status and an enum type order_status in the same schema collide. Use a table or an enum, not both.

docs.title: History, version and audit tables
docs.text: Table Meaning Why this name order_history Every past state of an order, as rows. _history for time-ordered copies. order_status_history Only the status changes of an order. Narrow the scope in the name. product_versions Every saved version of a product. _versions when users read old versions. document_revisions Edits of a document. _revisions for edit trails. price_changes One row per price change. A change log with a clear subject. audit_log Who changed what, for all tables. One shared log with a generic scope. order_archive Orders moved out of the live table. _archive for rows that left the live table. Prefer a deleted_at column unless rows must leave.

docs.title: Partition, event and queue tables
docs.text: Table Meaning Why this name orders_2026_11 The partition of orders for November 2026. The parent name plus the range. orders_2026_12 The next monthly partition. Same pattern, so partitions sort. orders_default Rows that match no other partition. _default for the catch-all. events_p0, events_p1 Hash partitions of events in PostgreSQL. p and the number. In MySQL, p0 is a partition name inside the table, not a table. outbox_events Events that wait to be published. The pattern name plus the content. job_queue Background jobs that wait to run. A container noun stays singular. webhook_deliveries Each attempt to call a webhook. A plural noun for events with a result.

docs.title: Bridge, fact and dimension tables
docs.text:
The prefixes fact_, dim_ and bridge_ name the role of the table in an analytics model. They do not repeat the object type, so they do not break the rule against prefixes. Some teams use dim_date (singular) and dbt projects often use fct_ for facts. Choose one form for the project.

Table Kind Meaning Why this name fact_orders Fact One row per order. fact_ marks a fact table. fact_order_items Fact One row per order line. A finer grain than fact_orders. dim_customers Dimension Customer attributes. dim_ marks a dimension. dim_products Dimension Product attributes. Same prefix. dim_dates Dimension One row per calendar day. A date dimension. bridge_order_promotions Bridge Links orders to many promotions. bridge_ links a fact to a multivalued dimension (Kimball).

docs.title: Bad → better
docs.text:
Bad Better Why tbl_orders orders A prefix repeats what the context shows. orders_table orders A suffix repeats the object type. Order orders PostgreSQL folds an unquoted Order to order, a reserved word, so queries fail. order_product (with quantity and price) order_items A link with data has a domain name. user_role_map user_roles map adds nothing. customer_invoice_data invoices data is filler, and the owner is clear. orders_old order_history or a partition orders_2025_12 old has no date and no meaning. orders_backup_final2 order_archive Version words in names rot. temp, test1 name the real purpose Never commit these. app_users (inside schema app) users The schema already gives the scope. statuses (a dictionary) order_status Lookup tables are singular in this guide. log audit_log or webhook_deliveries A bare log has no scope.

See also

  • Columns, Indexes, Constraints and Enums
  • Bad → better cookbook for more rewrites
  • Symmetry for pairs such as source and target

docs.title: Warehouse and analytics
docs.text:
General patterns

  • Name a table after its layer and its grain: the layer says how raw the data is, the grain says what one row is
  • Use snake_case for every object, as on the other database pages
  • Mark the role of a table with a prefix (stg_, int_, fact_, dim_, bridge_). Do not mark the object type
  • Use one key suffix for each key kind: _id for a source key, _key for a surrogate key. This split is for warehouse tables. Application tables follow Columns, where the surrogate key is id
  • Use _at for a timestamp and _date for a date, as in Columns

Useful tips

  • Decide plural or singular once. This page uses plural names (dim_customers). Some teams use singular (dim_customer) or fct_ for facts. Any one choice works if the project uses it everywhere
  • The dbt rules come from the dbt guides. Kimball sets the table roles and the ideas (grain, bridge, SCD), not name formats. The name formats on this page, such as _daily_snapshot, agg_, _key and the _loaded_at columns, are the choice of this guide

General anti-patterns

  • Names that hide the layer: orders_final, orders_new, orders_v2
  • Names that hide the grain: sales (one row per what?)
  • Mixed key suffixes: customer_id for a surrogate key in one table and for a source key in another

The examples use an e-commerce checkout. For the rules inside one table, see Tables and Columns.

docs.title: Layers
docs.text:
A warehouse moves data through steps. The two common naming systems differ, but they describe the same idea.

Step dbt layer Medallion layer What it holds 1 source bronze Raw copies of the source data. 2 staging (stg_) silver Clean and typed data, one table for each source table. 3 intermediate (int_) silver Joins and steps that are not for end users. This mapping to silver is approximate and is the choice of this guide. 4 marts gold Business tables for reports and tools.

See the dbt guide to project structure and the Databricks page on the medallion architecture.

docs.title: dbt model names
docs.text:
Layer Pattern Examples Why this name Staging stg_<source>__<entity> stg_shop__orders, stg_shop__order_items, stg_stripe__payments A double underscore splits the source from the entity. A single underscore splits words. Intermediate int_<entity>_<verb> int_orders_joined_to_payments, int_payments_pivoted_to_orders The verb says what the step does. Mart, entity <entity> orders, customers The dbt guide names marts after the business entity. Mart, with role prefix fact_<entity>, dim_<entity> fact_orders, dim_customers Use this form if the project follows Kimball. Source file _<folder>__sources.yml _shop__sources.yml The leading underscore keeps the file at the top of the folder. In staging, the folder is named after the source. Model file _<folder>__models.yml _marts__models.yml Same pattern. Snapshot <entity>_snapshot customers_snapshot The suffix shows that the table stores history. The dbt documentation uses this form in its examples. Seed <entity> country_codes, tax_rates A plain entity name, like a mart, because a seed is reference data. It is a small file in seeds/. Custom test assert_<expectation> assert_order_total_matches_item_sum The name states what must be true.

Staging models keep the source grain and do only light work: rename, cast and clean. See the dbt style guide, the page on snapshots and the page on seeds.

docs.title: Medallion names
docs.text:
Databricks uses a three-level name: catalog.schema.table. The medallion layers fit well as schema names.

Layer Pattern Examples Why this name Bronze bronze.<source>_<entity> bronze.shop_orders, bronze.stripe_payments The source is in the name. The data is raw. Silver silver.<entity> silver.orders, silver.customers Clean data has the business name. Gold gold.<report_or_entity> gold.daily_revenue, gold.customer_lifetime_value A gold table answers a business question. Environment the catalog prod.gold.daily_revenue, dev.gold.daily_revenue The catalog names the environment. The table name stays the same.

docs.title: Kimball tables
docs.text:
Kimball modeling puts measures in fact tables and descriptions in dimension tables.

Kind Pattern Examples Grain, or why this name Fact fact_<process> fact_orders One row per order. Fact, finer grain fact_<process>_<part> fact_order_items One row per order line. Periodic snapshot fact fact_<process>_daily_snapshot fact_inventory_daily_snapshot One row per product per day. Accumulating snapshot fact fact_<process>_lifecycle fact_order_fulfillment_lifecycle One row per order. The row updates as the order moves along. Dimension dim_<entity> dim_customers, dim_products, dim_stores One row per entity. Date dimension dim_dates dim_dates One row per calendar day. Junk dimension dim_<process>_flags dim_order_flags Holds low-cardinality flags in one table. Bridge bridge_<fact>_<dimension> bridge_order_promotions Links a fact to a multivalued dimension. Aggregate agg_<grain>_<measure> agg_daily_revenue, agg_monthly_orders_by_country A pre-computed summary. The grain is in the name.

docs.title: Keys
docs.text:
Kind Column pattern Examples Why this name Source (natural) key <entity>_id customer_id, order_id The key from the source system. Surrogate key <entity>_key customer_key, product_key A key made by the warehouse. A different suffix shows that it is not a source key. Date key, role-playing <role>_date_key order_date_key, ship_date_key Two roles of one dim_dates. The role is the prefix. Degenerate dimension the source number order_number An identifier that stays in the fact table. It has no dimension of its own. Unknown member a reserved key value, often -1 customer_key = -1 Kimball advises a default row for missing dimensions. The value -1 is a common choice.

A surrogate key can be a counter or a hash of the source key. The dbt_utils.generate_surrogate_key macro makes a hash. Name the column the same in the dimension and in every fact that uses it.

docs.title: History: SCD type 2
docs.text:
A slowly changing dimension of type 2 keeps one row for each version of an entity.

Column Type idea Meaning Why this name customer_key surrogate key One version of the customer. A new version gets a new key. customer_id source key The customer in the source system. It repeats in every version. valid_from timestamp When the version starts. A pair with valid_to. valid_to timestamp, nullable When the version ends. NULL means open. Document whether the end is included. is_current boolean The latest version. is_ marks a boolean, and the name is positive. dbt_valid_from, dbt_valid_to timestamp The same idea in a dbt snapshot. dbt makes these columns for you. dbt_updated_at, dbt_scd_id timestamp, text The change time and the row key in a dbt snapshot. dbt makes these too.

docs.title: Load and audit columns
docs.text: Column Meaning Why this name _loaded_at When the pipeline wrote the row. A leading underscore marks a technical column. _source_file The file that the row came from. Names the origin. _source_system The system that the row came from. Pairs with _source_file. _is_deleted The source deleted the row. is_ marks a boolean, and the underscore marks a technical column. _fivetran_synced, _fivetran_deleted The same ideas from the Fivetran connector. Keep the connector names in bronze. Rename them in staging.

docs.title: Bad → better
docs.text:
Bad Better Why orders_final fact_orders or orders A layer name tells more than a state word. stg_orders stg_shop__orders The source is in the name. A second source can have orders too. stg_shop_orders stg_shop__orders A double underscore splits the source from the entity. sales fact_order_items The grain is in the name. customer_dim dim_customers The role is the prefix, as in the other names. dim_customers.customer_id as a surrogate key customer_key One suffix for each key kind. is_latest_flag is_current is_ already marks a boolean, so flag adds nothing. start_date, end_date for versions valid_from, valid_to The pair has a clear meaning. tmp_orders_2 in a mart int_orders_joined_to_payments An intermediate step has a verb. daily agg_daily_revenue The grain and the measure are in the name.

See also

  • Tables, Columns and Constraints
  • Booleans, collections, units and time for _at, _date and units
  • Bad → better cookbook for more rewrites

docs.title: Examples by domain
docs.text:
General patterns

  • Use the words of the business. A name in the code is the same word that people use in the domain
  • Name the entity, then its states, then its actions. The three lists give the vocabulary of a domain
  • Check the traps. Most naming mistakes come from words that look the same and mean different things
  • Use the same name in the database, the API, the events and the code. See Systems and Databases

Useful tips

  • Start with a glossary of 10 to 20 terms before you write any code
  • Write down the states of the main entity as a list. Each state has one name and one meaning
  • Ask the domain experts when two words seem to mean the same. They often do not

General anti-patterns

  • Two names for one thing: customer and user for the same person
  • One name for two things: status for the state of an order and the state of a payment
  • A generic word where a domain word exists: item for an order line, type for a payment method

docs.title: What each page has
docs.text: Section What it gives Entities The nouns of the domain, with a short meaning. States The lifecycle of the main entities, one name for each state. Actions The verbs of the domain, in the form of a function name. Traps Words that are easy to confuse, with the better name. Worked example A small data model with SQL, API paths and code.

docs.title: Pages
docs.text:
Domain Page E-commerce E-commerce Payments Payments Fintech and banking Fintech and banking Healthcare Healthcare Logistics Logistics SaaS SaaS Machine learning Machine learning

See also

  • Naming patterns for the rules that hold in every domain
  • Languages for the case style of each language
  • References and glossary for sources and terms

docs.title: E-commerce
docs.text:
General patterns

  • Use customer for a person who buys. Use user only for a person who signs in to the system
  • Use order for a purchase that the customer has placed. Use cart before that
  • Give each entity its own state field and its own list of states. Do not mix the state of an order with the state of its payment
  • Use a past participle for a state (shipped) and a verb for an action (ship)
  • Store money in minor units with a currency code: total_amount_cents, currency_code

Useful tips

  • Name the money fields for what they hold: subtotal_amount_cents, tax_amount_cents, total_amount_cents
  • Keep payment, shipment and return as separate entities. Each has its own states
  • Pick one spelling for canceled and keep it. This guide uses canceled, as Stripe does. Shopify, Schema.org (OrderCancelled) and the glossary of this guide also show cancelled. If you map to one of those, keep their spelling in the mapped field
  • _cents assumes a currency with two decimals. For other currencies use _minor_units (see Columns)

General anti-patterns

  • item alone. It can mean a product, a variant, a cart item or an order item
  • status with no owner in code. Use order_status, payment_status, shipment_status for variables and fields in a DTO. Inside the orders table the column is just status
  • total alone. Name which total: before or after tax, discount and shipping
  • type for a payment method or a product kind

The states below are the choice of this guide. They map loosely to Stripe, Shopify and Schema.org, and they are not a copy of any of them.

docs.title: Entities
docs.text: Entity Meaning Table Notes Customer A person or company that buys. customers One row per buyer. Address A place. addresses The order points to a billing and a shipping address. Product What the shop sells, as a concept. products A shirt. Variant A product in a size or color. product_variants A blue shirt in size M. SKU The code that identifies a variant for stock. column sku A text code. Not a table. Category A group of products. categories Can nest. Price The price of a variant in a currency. prices Can change over time. Cart What a customer may buy. carts Before the order. Cart item One variant in a cart. cart_items Has a quantity. Order A purchase that the customer placed. orders Has a number and a state. Order item One variant in an order, with the price at that time. order_items The line of an order. Prices are copied here. Payment A charge for an order. payments An order can have many. Refund Money returned for a payment. refunds Linked to a payment. Shipment A group of packages sent together. shipments An order can have many. Package One physical box. packages Has a tracking number. Return Goods that come back. returns Has items and a reason. Coupon A discount that a customer enters as a code. coupons Has limits. Stripe splits it: Coupon is the rule and PromotionCode is the code. Promotion A rule that gives a discount with no code. promotions Applies by a condition. Shopify: an automatic discount. Stock level How many units are in a place. stock_levels One row per variant and warehouse. Warehouse A place where stock is kept. warehouses Review A customer's rating of a product. reviews Tax rate A rule for tax by place and product. tax_rates

docs.title: Order
docs.text:
The order states cover the work on the order. The money is in the payment states below.

State Meaning Next states pending The order is placed. Payment may be open. processing, on_hold, canceled processing The shop prepares the goods. partially_shipped, shipped, on_hold, canceled on_hold The shop stopped the order for a check. processing, canceled partially_shipped Some goods are with the carrier. shipped shipped All goods are with the carrier. delivered delivered The customer has the goods. completed completed The order is closed and no return is open. none canceled The order was stopped before shipping. none

A return does not change the order state. It has its own states. A refund changes the payment state.

docs.title: Payment, shipment and return
docs.text:
Entity State Meaning Next states Payment pending The payment waits for the customer or the bank. authorized, failed authorized The funds are held. captured, voided captured The funds are taken. partially_refunded, refunded failed The bank refused. none voided The hold was released. none partially_refunded Some money was returned. refunded refunded All money was returned. none Shipment label_created The carrier label exists. in_transit in_transit The carrier has the package. out_for_delivery, delivered, delivery_failed out_for_delivery The package is on the last leg. delivered, delivery_failed delivery_failed The carrier could not deliver. in_transit, returned_to_sender delivered The package arrived. none returned_to_sender The package went back to the shop. none Return requested The customer asked for a return. approved, rejected approved The shop accepts the return. received rejected The shop refuses the return. closed received The goods came back. closed closed The return is finished. A refund may follow. none

Words differ by platform. Stripe has no captured state for a payment intent (captured is a flag on a charge). Stripe cancels an uncaptured payment, and voided is the word of Shopify and Braintree. Shopify names the return states REQUESTED, OPEN, CLOSED, CANCELED and DECLINED.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text: Action Function name Meaning Trap Add a variant to a cart add_item_to_cart Creates or changes a cart item. Do not use add_to_cart. Remove a variant from a cart remove_item_from_cart Deletes a cart item. In the API it is DELETE /v1/carts/{cart_id}/items/{item_id}. Apply a coupon apply_coupon Checks and adds a discount. redeem_coupon marks it as used. Place an order place_order Turns a cart into an order. The API route is POST /v1/carts/{cart_id}:checkout. Authorize a payment authorize_payment Holds the money. Not the same as capture. Capture a payment capture_payment Takes the held money. Void a payment void_payment Releases a hold before capture. Not a refund. Cancel an order cancel_order Stops an order before shipping. If the order is paid, also void or refund the payment. After shipping, use a return. Reserve stock reserve_stock Holds units for an order. Release stock release_stock Frees held units. Ship an order ship_order Creates a shipment and hands the goods to a carrier. The shipment has its own states. Record a delivery record_shipment_delivered Sets the shipment to delivered. The carrier webhook calls it. Request a return request_return Starts a return. Approve a return approve_return The shop accepts the return. Reject a return reject_return The shop refuses the return. Receive a return receive_return Records that the goods came back. Refund a payment refund_payment Returns money. After capture only. Restock a return restock_return Adds returned units to stock. Only for goods that can be sold again.

docs.title: Traps
docs.text: Trap Why it is a problem Better order as a column or a word order is a reserved SQL word. It also means "sort". orders for the table. purchase_order for a buyer's order to a supplier. canceled and cancelled Two spellings in one code base. One spelling. This guide uses canceled. cancel, void, refund Three ways to stop a payment. void before capture, refund after capture, cancel for the order. status and state Two words for one idea. status in names, state in text about state machines. total Before or after tax, discount and shipping? subtotal_amount_cents, total_amount_cents. price, amount, cost Three words for money. price is what the buyer pays per unit. amount is a computed total on a record. cost is what the shop pays. product, variant, sku, item Four words for what is sold. product for the concept, variant for the sellable unit, sku for its code, order_item for a line. customer, user, account Three words for a person. customer buys. user signs in. Avoid account for a buyer. In Stripe, account is the seller. address Billing or shipping? billing_address_id, shipping_address_id. shipment, delivery, fulfillment Three words for sending goods. shipment for the group of packages, delivered_at for the event. fulfillment is the whole pick, pack and ship process. Shopify also uses it for a shipment. stock, inventory, quantity Three words for units. stock_level for the entity, quantity for a count in an item. discount, coupon, promotion Three words for a lower price. coupon has a code. promotion has a rule. discount_amount_cents is the result. paid_at Authorized or captured? authorized_at, captured_at. return as a variable return is a keyword in many languages. return_request or product_return for a variable. Return or ProductReturn for a class. returns for the table.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
The data model in SQL. The table product_variants is not shown.

CREATE TABLE customers (
    id          bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY,
    email       text NOT NULL,

A cancel of a paid order sends OrderCanceled. The payment service listens to it and then sends PaymentRefunded, or voids the hold.

The code:

from enum import Enum


class OrderStatus(str, Enum):
    PENDING = "pending"
    PROCESSING = "processing"
    ON_HOLD = "on_hold"
    PARTIALLY_SHIPPED = "partially_shipped"
    SHIPPED = "shipped"
    DELIVERED = "delivered"
    COMPLETED = "completed"
    CANCELED = "canceled"


CANCELABLE_ORDER_STATUSES = {OrderStatus.PENDING, OrderStatus.PROCESSING, OrderStatus.ON_HOLD}


def place_order(cart: Cart) -> Order:
    order_items = [build_order_item(cart_item) for cart_item in cart.cart_items]
    subtotal_amount_cents = sum(order_item.unit_price_cents * order_item.quantity for order_item in order_items)
    tax_amount_cents = calculate_tax_amount_cents(order_items, cart.shipping_address)
    return Order(
        customer_id=cart.customer_id,
        order_items=order_items,
        order_status=OrderStatus.PENDING,
        subtotal_amount_cents=subtotal_amount_cents,
        tax_amount_cents=tax_amount_cents,
        total_amount_cents=subtotal_amount_cents + tax_amount_cents,
        currency_code=cart.currency_code,
        placed_at=utc_now(),
    )


def can_cancel_order(order: Order) -> bool:
    return order.order_status in CANCELABLE_ORDER_STATUSES

docs.title: Fintech and banking
docs.text:
General patterns

  • Name the ledger parts with the words of accounting: account, ledger_entry, journal, balance
  • Record each money change as a new entry. Never change an old entry
  • Use debit and credit as the two sides of an entry. Do not use plus and minus
  • Keep the amount in minor units with a currency code: amount_cents, currency_code
  • Give the booking date and the value date their own names: booked_at, value_date

Useful tips

  • Name a balance for the moment it describes: available_balance_cents, ledger_balance_cents, pending_balance_cents
  • Use posted_at for the time a journal becomes final, and created_at for the time you wrote the row. booked_at is a timestamp here and value_date is a date. ISO 20022 uses dates for both, so use booking_date if you need only the date
  • Use a reference that a person can read: end_to_end_id, statement_reference
  • Name the unit of a rate: interest_rate_percent (4.5 means 4.5%) or interest_rate_bps. A plain _rate is a 0-to-1 ratio or an exchange rate, such as fx_rate

General anti-patterns

  • balance with no kind. Available or ledger?
  • transaction for a ledger entry, a database transaction and a payment at the same time
  • amount that can be negative with no rule for the sign
  • date for the booking date, the value date and the creation date
  • A float for money: balance = 10.1

The words come from double-entry bookkeeping, from ISO 20022 and from the vocabulary of retail banks. Names for the bank to customer messages are in Payments.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text: Action Function name Meaning Trap Open an account open_account Creates an account. create_account may skip KYC. Close an account close_account Ends an account. The balance must be zero. Freeze an account freeze_account Blocks debits. Credits may still come in, by policy. Post a journal post_journal Checks that the journal balances and makes it final. Post a whole journal, never one entry. Reverse a journal reverse_journal Adds a new journal that cancels an old one. Never delete. The new journal has reverses_journal_id. Initiate a transfer initiate_transfer Starts a transfer. Book a transfer book_transfer Creates the journal with its entries. Settle a transfer settle_transfer Records the final exchange. Return a payment return_payment The receiver bank sends the money back. Not a refund. Accrue interest accrue_interest Adds the daily interest. docs.title: Traps
docs.text: Trap Why it is a problem Better balance Available, ledger or pending? available_balance_cents, ledger_balance_cents. transaction A ledger entry, a database transaction and a bank event share the word. ledger_entry, bank_transaction, db_transaction. debit and credit as signs Debit means an increase on an asset account and a decrease on a liability account. A side column with debit or credit, and a positive amount. amount with a sign Plus and minus differ by bank. amount_cents positive, and the side in side. date Booking date, value date or creation date? booked_at, value_date, created_at. booked and posted and settled Three stages that look alike. In ISO 20022 camt messages, BOOK (booked) already means final and PDNG means pending. This guide's convention: booked when the transfer is recorded, posted when its journal is final in the ledger, settled when the money moved between banks. Say which meaning you use. reverse and refund and return A reverse is an accounting move. A refund is a business act. A return is an interbank message. reverse_journal, refund_charge, return_payment. account A customer account or a ledger account? On this page account is the customer account. Use ledger_account for the books. When both exist in one system, write customer_account in full. iban as a key It can change. A surrogate id and a unique iban. interest Rate, accrual or paid amount? interest_rate_percent, interest_accrued_cents, interest_paid_cents. fee and charge Charge also means a card payment. fee for a bank cost, charge for a card payment. currency A code or a symbol? currency_code with ISO 4217. rate Interest rate or FX rate? interest_rate_percent, fx_rate.

The service also checks that the currency of each entry equals the currency of its ledger account.

from collections import defaultdict


def post_journal(journal: Journal) -> None:
    if len(journal.entries) < 2:
        raise UnbalancedJournalError(journal.id, {})
    balance_cents_by_currency: dict[str, int] = defaultdict(int)
    for entry in journal.entries:
        sign = 1 if entry.side == "debit" else -1
        balance_cents_by_currency[entry.currency_code] += sign * entry.amount_cents
    if any(balance_cents != 0 for balance_cents in balance_cents_by_currency.values()):
        raise UnbalancedJournalError(journal.id, dict(balance_cents_by_currency))
    journal.mark_posted(posted_at=utc_now())

docs.title: Healthcare
docs.text:
General patterns

  • Use the names of HL7 FHIR for the clinical entities: Patient, Encounter, Observation, Condition, MedicationRequest
  • Keep the request, the event and the result as separate entities: MedicationRequest, MedicationAdministration, Observation
  • Store a coded value as a system, a code and a display text: code_system, code, display
  • Give each resource that has a status the FHIR value set, and a way to mark a wrong entry: entered_in_error
  • Keep the clinical time and the record time apart: effective_at, recorded_at

Useful tips

  • Use patient_id in every table that holds clinical data. Do not use a name or a birth date as a key
  • Use a full coding system for a code: LOINC for tests, SNOMED CT for findings, ICD-10 for diagnoses, RxNorm for drugs
  • Write units with UCUM codes: mg, mmol/L, mm[Hg]
  • Treat the name and the identifiers of a patient as personal data. Keep real values out of the names of tables, columns, indexes and constraints, out of logs and out of URLs

General anti-patterns

  • patient_name as an identifier
  • diagnosis as free text with no code
  • visit for an appointment, an encounter and an admission at once
  • result for the test, the value and the report
  • Deleting a wrong record. Mark it entered_in_error

The names follow the HL7 FHIR resources (release R4 and R5). FHIR resource names are UpperCamelCase. In a JSON message the field names are lowerCamelCase, for example birthDate. This page uses snake_case for database columns, as in Columns. Map the names in one place.

docs.title: Logistics
docs.text:
General patterns

  • Name the contract, the physical goods and the movement as separate entities: consignment, parcel, shipment
  • Name a tracking fact as an event: tracking_event, with a type, a time, a place and a status
  • Use the words of the standard in your field. GS1 EPCIS uses what, when, where, why for each event
  • Keep the planned time and the actual time apart: planned_at, actual_at, or estimated_delivery_at and delivered_at
  • Store weight and size with the unit in the name: weight_grams, length_millimeters

Useful tips

  • Use a global code for places and goods: GLN for a location, GTIN for a product, SSCC for a pallet or another logistic unit
  • Give each leg of a route its own record. One shipment can have many legs
  • Use UN/LOCODE for a port or a city, and ISO 3166 for a country
  • Use the incoterm as a code: incoterm_code with DAP, DDP, FOB

General anti-patterns

  • shipment for the order, the box and the trip at once
  • status that mixes the transport state and the customs state
  • weight with no unit
  • address as one free-text column for the sender, the receiver and the depot
  • delivered set by a person, not by a delivery event

The examples use the words of carriers and of GS1 EPCIS. EPCIS is a standard for events about objects in a supply chain. Its event types are ObjectEvent, AggregationEvent, TransactionEvent, TransformationEvent and AssociationEvent.

A shipment on this page is one transport of goods. In E-commerce a shipment is a group of packages sent together, and the tracking number is on the package. Carrier systems often keep the number on the shipment. Pick one owner for the number and keep it. This page names the first state created, where the e-commerce page uses label_created. The shipment owns the state delivered, and a parcel scan updates it.
