docs.title: Symmetry
docs.text:
When two names describe opposite or matching sides of one idea, make them look like a pair. A reader who knows open_session can then guess close_session. This page lists pairs, shows how to choose one pair for one idea, and shows mismatched pairs to avoid.

General patterns

  • Use the exact opposite word: price_min and price_max, lock_cart and unlock_cart.
  • Keep the pair at the same length and in the same form: starts_at and ends_at, not starts_at and finish_time.
  • Choose one pair for one idea and use it in the whole code base: source/target, or source/destination, but not both.
  • Put the shared part first, so that the pair sorts together: shipping_from, shipping_to. See Action and context.
  • Use the same verb forms for both sides of an action pair: add_item and remove_item, not add_item and delete_item_from_cart.
  • Name a range with its bounds: price_min and price_max, or valid_from and valid_to. The glossary uses the suffix form _min and _max.

Useful tips

  • When you add a function, ask "What undoes this?" Then name the second function now, even if you write it later.
  • State in the name or in the docs whether a bound is inclusive. For example, write valid_from and valid_to and document that the start is included and the end is not.
  • Standard libraries often give you the pair. Python locks use acquire() and release(). Many SQL databases use BEGIN, COMMIT and ROLLBACK.
  • For negative names, see Negation and optionality.

General anti-patterns

  • Half pairs: open_session() with shutdown_session(). Use close_session().
  • Different words for the same side: start_date in one table and begin_date in another.
  • Pairs that are close but not opposite: price_min with highest_price. Use price_max.
  • Two pairs for one idea: source/target in one module and origin/destination in another.

docs.title: Range and bounds
docs.text: Pair Example identifiers Why min / max quantity_min, quantity_max The exact opposite of the lowest value is the highest value. Suffix form, as in the glossary. lower / upper lower_bound, upper_bound Use for the edges of an interval. from / to valid_from, valid_to A range between two points. starts / ends starts_at, ends_at Moments of an event: same suffix _at. before / after placed_before, placed_after Filters on a moment. since / until since_date, until_date The start and the end of a period. Say in the docs if the end is included.

docs.title: Position and order
docs.text: Pair Example identifiers Why first / last first_item, last_item Positions in an ordered group. head / tail queue_head, queue_tail Ends of a queue or a list. previous / next previous_page, next_page Neighbours in a sequence. parent / child parent_category, child_category Levels in a tree. left / right left_node, right_node Sides of a binary tree. top / bottom top_offset, bottom_offset Vertical sides in layout code.

docs.title: Direction and flow
docs.text: Pair Example identifiers Why source / target source_warehouse, target_warehouse Where data or goods leave and arrive. sender / recipient sender_address, recipient_address The two parties in a message or parcel. producer / consumer order_producer, order_consumer The two ends of a queue. inbound / outbound inbound_shipment, outbound_shipment Direction relative to your system. request / response payment_request, payment_response A call and its answer. upload / download upload_invoice, download_invoice Direction relative to the client. import / export import_catalog, export_catalog Data moves into or out of the system. send / receive send_notice, receive_notice Sides of one transfer.

docs.title: Lifecycle and state
docs.text: Pair Example identifiers Why open / close open_session, close_session A resource that you must release. start / stop start_worker, stop_worker A process. pause / resume pause_subscription, resume_subscription A process that continues later. enable / disable enable_feature, disable_feature A switch. lock / unlock lock_cart, unlock_cart A state flag on a record. acquire / release acquire_lock, release_lock Take and give back a shared resource, such as a lock or a connection. activate / deactivate activate_coupon, deactivate_coupon A record that changes state. connect / disconnect connect_gateway, disconnect_gateway A link.

docs.title: Collections and records
docs.text: Pair Example identifiers Why add / remove add_item, remove_item Change a collection. create / delete create_order, delete_order Change a stored record. include / exclude include_tax, exclude_tax A filter or a choice. attach / detach attach_label, detach_label Link and unlink two records. register / unregister register_webhook, unregister_webhook Add and remove a listener. subscribe / unsubscribe subscribe_to_newsletter, unsubscribe_from_newsletter A feed. load / save load_cart, save_cart Move a record from and to storage.

docs.title: Transform and security
docs.text: Pair Example identifiers Why encode / decode encode_cursor, decode_cursor A reversible change of format. serialize / deserialize serialize_order, deserialize_order Object to text and back. compress / decompress compress_export, decompress_export A reversible size change. encrypt / decrypt encrypt_card_token, decrypt_card_token A reversible secret. grant / revoke grant_role, revoke_role A permission. allow / deny allow_list, deny_list A rule list.

docs.title: Money and transactions
docs.text: Pair Example identifiers Why debit / credit debit_account, credit_account The two sides of an accounting entry. authorize / void authorize_payment, void_authorization Hold money, then release the hold. Gateways differ. Stripe Payment Intents use capture to take the money and cancel on the intent. See Stripe Payment Intents. begin / commit / rollback begin_transaction, commit_transaction, rollback_transaction Common SQL commands. PostgreSQL uses BEGIN. Standard SQL spells it START TRANSACTION. See PostgreSQL BEGIN. buy / sell buy_order, sell_order The two sides of a trade. charge / refund charge_order, refund_order Take money and give it back.

docs.title: Mismatched pairs
docs.text: Bad Better Why start_date / finish_time starts_at / ends_at Different words and different types. If you need a date, use starts_on and ends_on. begin_session() / shutdown_session() open_session() / close_session() The second word is not the opposite of the first. add_item() / delete_item() add_item() / remove_item() add and remove change a collection. create and delete change a stored record. price_min / highest_price price_min / price_max highest is not the exact opposite of min. enable_feature() / turn_off_feature() enable_feature() / disable_feature() One word family for both sides. source_warehouse in one module, origin_warehouse in another source_warehouse everywhere Either pair works. Do not use both. first_page / end_page first_page / last_page first pairs with last. lock_cart() / open_cart() lock_cart() / unlock_cart() open does not undo lock. from_date / end_date from_date / to_date Two words of the same type. sender_address in one module, from_address in another sender_address / recipient_address One word for each side in the whole code base. parent_id / kid_id parent_id / child_id Use the standard word. encrypt_token() / unlock_token() encrypt_token() / decrypt_token() unlock belongs to lock.

docs.title: General rules
docs.text:
Python is a dynamically typed language — you can assign different types to the same variable. Avoid it by any means. Type annotations are your primary defence.

PEP 8 naming at a glance

Entity Convention Example Variables snake_case user_name, order_total Functions snake_case fetch_orders(), validate_email() Classes CamelCase OrderProcessor, Customer Exceptions CamelCase + Error/Warning suffix PaymentError, DeprecationWarning Constants UPPER_SNAKE_CASE MAX_RETRIES, DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS Modules snake_case email_sender.py Packages lowercase, no underscores payment, order_processing Type variables short CamelCase T, T_co, K, V

Useful tips

  • Use type annotations for every function signature — they serve as documentation and enable static analysis
  • Use TypeVar with descriptive names for generic types: T = TypeVar("T"), T_co = TypeVar("T_co", covariant=True), K = TypeVar("K") for keys, V = TypeVar("V") for values
  • Use conventional aliases for popular libraries: import pandas as pd, import numpy as np, import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
  • Use TYPE_CHECKING guard for type-only imports to avoid circular dependencies: from __future__ import annotations is often simpler
  • Prefer from __future__ import annotations at the top of every file — it makes all annotations strings (faster, no forward-reference issues)
  • Prefix non-public names with a single underscore: _internal_helper(), _cache_size. Double underscore __name_mangling is rarely needed — reserve it for mixins and base classes to avoid name clashes
  • Use _ as a throwaway name for unpacking: key, _, value = partition("a=b")

General anti-patterns

  • Using from module import * — pollutes the namespace and makes the source of names invisible
  • Overusing __double_underscore on every private attribute — prefer _single_underscore unless you specifically need name mangling
  • Ignoring type annotations in public APIs — callers have no way to know what types to pass

docs.title: Method patterns
docs.text: The tables use an e-commerce checkout. For function names outside classes, see Functions. For class names, see Classes.

docs.title: Mutating and non-mutating
docs.text:
A method that changes the object and a method that returns a changed copy need different names. Python itself shows the pair: list.sort() changes the list and returns None, and sorted() returns a new list.

Mutates the object Returns a new object Why cart.add_item(item) cart.with_item(item) add changes the cart. with_ returns a changed copy. order.apply_coupon(code) order.with_coupon(code) The with_ form is safe for frozen objects. cart.sort_items() cart.sorted_items() The Python pair: sort changes, sorted returns. cart.reverse_items() cart.reversed_items() reverse changes the list in place. reversed() returns an iterator, so reversed_items() should return a new list. address.normalize() address.normalized() The past participle marks a new, normalized copy. The original stays unchanged. cart.attach_note(text) cart.with_note(text) pathlib uses with_name and with_suffix for the same idea.

Rule of thumb

  • A method that changes the object uses an imperative verb: sort, add, clear. The reverse is not true: calculate_tax is a verb and does not change the object.
  • A past participle or a with_ prefix returns a new object: sorted, normalized, with_item.
  • A mutating method usually returns None. Do not return self unless the class is a builder.

docs.title: Conversions
docs.text: Pattern Use it when Examples to_<target> The object converts itself. order.to_dict(), money.to_decimal(), address.to_label() as_<view> The method is a thin wrapper over the same data. This is a project convention, not a Python rule. cart.as_read_only(), order.as_line_items() to_summary The method builds a new summary object. order.to_summary() from_<source> A class method builds an object from another shape. Order.from_cart(cart), Money.from_cents(1999, "EUR"), Address.from_dict(data) parse A class method reads text. CouponCode.parse("SAVE10"), Money.parse("19.99 EUR") <source>_to_<target> A function converts between two other types. cart_to_order, order_to_invoice

docs.title: Predicates
docs.text:
Pattern Use it when Examples is_<state>() The method checks a state. order.is_paid(), cart.is_empty(), coupon.is_expired() has_<thing>() The method checks ownership. order.has_discount(), customer.has_saved_card() can_<action>() The method checks ability. order.can_cancel(), payment.can_refund() should_<action>() The method checks a decision. payment.should_retry(), order.should_ship()

A predicate returns a bool and does not change the object. A cheap predicate without arguments may be a property (order.is_paid). Use a method (order.can_cancel()) when the check takes arguments or does work. Pick one form per code base, because a forgotten () on a method makes if order.is_paid: always true. See Booleans, collections, units and time.

docs.title: Properties and methods
docs.text: Use a property when Use a method when Examples The value is cheap and has no arguments. The work costs time or needs arguments. order.total_cents and order.calculate_tax(region) The name is a noun. The name is a verb. cart.item_count and cart.merge(other_cart) Reading has no side effect. The call has a side effect or does input and output. customer.full_name and customer.send_welcome_email() The value looks like a field. The call may fail or wait. order.status and order.fetch_tracking()

docs.title: Dunder methods
docs.text:
Python reserves the names with double underscores at both ends. Use the standard ones. Do not invent names of the form __something__, such as __calc__.

Method Purpose Example __init__ Set up a new instance. Order, Cart __post_init__ Check or derive fields after a dataclass __init__. Money __repr__ Show a developer-friendly text. Order(id=7, status="paid") __str__ Show a human-friendly text. Address as a label __eq__ Compare for equality. Money __hash__ Make the object hashable for sets and dict keys. Define it with __eq__, on an immutable class. Money, Address __len__ Return the number of items. Cart __iter__ Loop over the items. Cart, Order __contains__ Support in. Cart with sku in cart __enter__ / __exit__ Support with. CheckoutSession __call__ Make the object callable. PricingStrategy

See also Special functions.

docs.title: classmethod and staticmethod
docs.text:
Kind Naming rule Examples @classmethod constructor from_<source>, parse, or a noun for a named instance. Order.from_cart, Money.zero, Address.parse @classmethod named instance A noun for the instance. Use create_ only if the method stores the object. Coupon.percent_off(10), Order.draft() @staticmethod helper Name it by what it checks or computes. No self, no cls. Sku.is_valid_format(text), Money.round_to_cents(value) Module function Use it when the code needs no class. order_to_invoice(order)

If a static method has no real tie to the concept of the class, make it a module-level function.

docs.title: Bad → better
docs.text:
Bad Better Why cart.get_sorted() that sorts in place cart.sort_items() The name must match the change. cart.sort() that returns a copy cart.sorted_items() sort suggests a change in place. order.paid() order.is_paid() The prefix shows a boolean. order.total() that reads a stored field order.total_cents (property) A cheap value fits a property. customer.get_name() customer.name (property) Python style prefers attributes and properties to getters. order.convert() order.to_invoice() Name the target. Order.make(cart) Order.from_cart(cart) from_ is the common name for an alternative constructor. Money.parse_static() Money.parse() Do not put the decorator in the name. order.__calc__() order.calculate_total() Do not invent dunder names. cart.items_count() cart.item_count (property) A count is cheap and noun-like.

docs.title: Classes
docs.text:
General patterns

  • Use CamelCase in the class names
  • The class represents an object with a complex, encapsulated (or not) functionality. Use nouns to reflect it.

Useful tips

  • Use a consistent naming convention throughout your code, so it's easy to understand and navigate. If you're working on a team, agree on a naming convention to use across all your code.
  • Class names should be concise and easy to type, but also descriptive enough to convey their purpose. Avoid excessively long names that are difficult to read or type.
  • Use mnemonics: If your class name is hard to remember or pronounce, consider using a mnemonic or an acronym to help people remember it. Just make sure the mnemonic or acronym is easy to understand and related to the purpose of the class.
  • When choosing a class name, consider the future scalability of your code. Choose a name that can easily accommodate potential future changes or additions to your code, without requiring a complete rewrite.

General anti-patterns

  • Avoid using abbreviations in your class names, unless they are commonly understood within your domain. Abbreviations can be confusing and make your code harder to read.
  • Avoid the Manager or Service suffix on every class — not every class manages something. Use precise suffixes: Validator, Builder, Parser, Gateway, Mapper
  • Avoid including a pattern name in the class name unless the pattern is the public API: UserFactory is fine; UserSingletonFactoryProxy is not
  • Avoid Utils / Helper classes — they are dumping grounds for unrelated logic. Split into domain-specific classes

docs.title: Suffix glossary
docs.text:
A suffix tells the reader the role of the class. Use a suffix only when the class really has that role. The examples use an e-commerce checkout.

Suffix Use it when Example Avoid Validator The class checks input against rules and reports problems. OrderValidator, AddressValidator OrderChecker next to OrderValidator Parser The class reads text into a structure. CouponCodeParser, PriceParser PriceReader Serializer The class turns an object into a transfer format and back. OrderSerializer, InvoiceSerializer OrderConverter for the same job Builder The class builds a complex object step by step. InvoiceBuilder, SearchQueryBuilder InvoiceMaker Factory The class creates objects of a family or picks the type. PaymentMethodFactory, NotifierFactory A factory that only calls a constructor Repository The class stores and loads one kind of record, like a collection. OrderRepository, CustomerRepository OrderManager, OrderDao in the same code base Gateway The class is the domain-facing entry to an external system. PaymentGateway, ShippingGateway PaymentHelper Client The class is the low-level caller of a remote API. TaxApiClient, CarrierApiClient Client alone Adapter The class implements one interface on top of another system. LegacyOrderAdapter, StripeAdapter Wrapper Mapper The class converts between two models. OrderMapper, AddressMapper OrderUtil Policy The class holds one business rule that can change. RefundPolicy, FreeShippingPolicy Rule flags spread over many functions Strategy The class is one swappable algorithm. FlatRateShippingStrategy, PercentDiscountStrategy ShippingType with if chains Handler The class receives a raw message, a webhook or a command. CancelOrderHandler, PaymentWebhookHandler OrderHandler for everything Controller The class receives web requests and calls the code that runs the use cases. OrderController, CartController A controller that holds business rules Listener The class reacts to one named event. OrderCreatedListener, PaymentFailedListener OrderObserver next to OrderListener Publisher The class sends events to subscribers. OrderEventPublisher, PaymentEventPublisher OrderNotifier for event publishing Provider The class supplies a value or a dependency on request, such as the current time or a rate. TaxRateProvider, ClockProvider A Factory that builds domain objects Registry The class holds named entries for lookup. PaymentMethodRegistry, HandlerRegistry A bare module-level dict changed from many places Resolver The class maps a symbolic name or key to a concrete target by rules, such as aliases or fallbacks. It is not a store: use Repository for records by id. TaxRuleResolver, CarrierResolver Finder Coordinator The class runs several collaborators in one workflow. CheckoutCoordinator, RefundCoordinator CheckoutManager Processor The class is a stage in a pipeline that transforms items. ReceiptLineProcessor, ImageResizeProcessor Processor for any class that has a process method Engine The class is a core component that runs complex logic by its own rules. PricingEngine, RuleEngine Engine for a small helper Job The class is scheduled or recurring work. Do not use both Job and Task in one code base. ExpireCartsJob, SendDigestJob CartCleanup Worker The class is a process or thread that runs jobs. EmailWorker, ImportWorker Runner Task The class is one queued unit of work. SendReceiptTask, SyncStockTask Task for a plain function Command The object is a request to change something. CancelOrderCommand, ApplyCouponCommand CancelOrderData Query The object is a request to read something. ListOpenOrdersQuery, ListRefundsQuery OrderFilterData Result The object is the outcome of an operation. RefundResult, ValidationResult A bare tuple Snapshot The object is a frozen copy at one time. OrderSnapshot, PriceSnapshot Order2 Config The object holds the settings of one component. GatewayConfig, RetryConfig Both Settings and Config in one code base Options The object holds optional parameters of one call. SearchOptions, ExportOptions Params Context The object holds data shared during one call or request. CheckoutContext, RequestContext Context for any dict Session The object holds the state of one interaction with a start and an end. ShoppingSession, CheckoutSession Session for a user record State The type represents the states of a state machine. OrderState, PaymentState Both Status and State for the same concept in one code base Cursor The object marks a position in a sequence. OrderCursor, EventCursor Pointer Page The object is one slice of a paged result. OrderPage, ProductPage OrderList Dto The object carries data across a boundary and has no behaviour. OrderDto, CustomerDto OrderData

Acronyms in class names

PEP 8 asks for all letters of an acronym in capitals in CapWords, as in HTTPServerError, so OrderDTO and TaxAPIClient follow PEP 8. The examples on this page use Dto, Api and Id on purpose, for readability. Choose one form and keep it in the whole code base. See Abbreviations.

docs.title: Manager and Service
docs.text:
Manager and Service are the most overused suffixes. Use them with care.

Suffix Fine when Better when Examples Service The class holds domain logic that fits no entity, and the name states the domain. The class is mostly a wrapper around one entity or one store. PricingService is fine. Use OrderRepository for storage. Manager Rarely. A framework may require it. The class has a real job. OrderManager (schedules orders) → OrderScheduler. (Stores orders) → OrderRepository. (Runs the checkout steps) → CheckoutCoordinator. Helper, Util, Utils Never. Split the class by job, or use module functions. OrderUtil → module order_rules

docs.text:
The base class or the decorator also shapes the name.

Kind Naming rule Examples Protocol Name the capability. Use an adjective, an -able word or a Supports prefix. Refundable, SupportsRefund, Cancellable ABC Use a plain noun for the contract. Avoid Abstract as a prefix unless the code base already uses it. PaymentMethod, ShippingCarrier Mixin End the name with Mixin. Name the added ability. TimestampMixin, SoftDeleteMixin, AuditMixin @dataclass Use a singular noun for the record. Add frozen=True for a value object. OrderLine, Address, Money TypedDict Name the shape of the payload. OrderPayload, CouponPayload NamedTuple Use a short noun for a small fixed record. PriceRange, GeoPoint Generic Use a short CapWords name for a type variable, such as T or KeyT. Add _co or _contra for variance. Name the class for its job. T, OrderT, Repository[OrderT] Enum Use a singular noun. Members are upper case. See Enums. OrderStatus, ShippingMethod Exception End the name with Error (Warning for warnings). See Exceptions. PaymentDeclinedError, OutOfStockError NewType Name the meaning of the id or the value. The string must match the name: OrderId = NewType("OrderId", int). OrderId, CustomerId, CurrencyCode

docs.title: Constants
docs.text:
General patterns

  • Use UPPER_SNAKE_CASE for all module-level constants: MAX_RETRIES = 3, DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 30
  • Prefix internal (non-exported) constants with a single underscore: _INTERNAL_CACHE_SIZE = 1024
  • Group related constants into classes or frozen dataclasses when they form a logical set
  • Type-annotate constants for better IDE support: API_BASE_URL: str = "https://example.com"

Useful tips

  • Place constants at the top of the module, right after imports
  • Use Final from typing to signal a constant is not meant to be reassigned: from typing import Final; MAX_CONNECTIONS: Final[int] = 10
  • For domain-specific numeric values, include the unit in the name: TIMEOUT_MS, BUFFER_SIZE_KB
  • Prefer enum.Enum or enum.StrEnum over a module full of string constants when values belong together

General anti-patterns

  • Lowercase or mixed-case constant names: max_retries = 3 (looks like a regular variable)
  • Magic literals scattered through code — they should be named constants
  • Spreading related constants across unrelated modules
  • Using a dict instead of a class or enum for a fixed set of related constants (loses type safety)
from typing import Final

API_BASE_URL: Final[str] = "https://api.example.com/v2"
DEFAULT_PAGE_SIZE: Final[int] = 50
MAX_UPLOAD_SIZE_MB: Final[int] = 100
REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS: Final[int] = 5000

# Related constants grouped in a frozen dataclass
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class PaginationDefaults:
    size: int = 20
    max_size: int = 100
    starting_page: int = 1

docs.title: Enums
docs.text:
General patterns

  • Use CamelCase for the enum class name
  • Use UPPER_SNAKE_CASE for enum members (PEP 8 convention): class Color(Enum): RED = 1; GREEN = 2
  • If you need to mix enums with string values, inherit from StrEnum
  • Use auto() when the exact value is irrelevant: class Priority(IntEnum): LOW = auto(); MEDIUM = auto(); HIGH = auto()

Useful tips

  • Use IntEnum when enum values participate in numeric operations or comparisons with integers
  • Use StrEnum when your enums represent string constants and need to compare cleanly with strings
  • Add a __str__ or @property for human-readable labels: class Status(Enum): ACTIVE = 1; @property def label(self): ...
  • If a boolean flag is better expressed as an enum, prefer the enum for extensibility: ConnectionMode.SSL vs is_secure=True

General anti-patterns

  • Mixing member naming styles within the same enum class
  • Assigning arbitrary or meaningless values when auto() would suffice
  • Using a plain class with module-level constants instead of Enum (loses iteration, type-safety, and repr)
  • Naming the class in snake_case: class connection_mode(Enum): (should be ConnectionMode)
from enum import Enum, auto, IntEnum, StrEnum

class OrderStatus(Enum):
    PENDING = auto()
    CONFIRMED = auto()
    SHIPPED = auto()
    DELIVERED = auto()
    CANCELLED = auto()

    @property
    def label(self) -> str:
        return self.name.title()

class Priority(IntEnum):
    LOW = 10
    MEDIUM = 50
    HIGH = 100
    CRITICAL = 200

class ShippingMethod(StrEnum):
    STANDARD = "standard"
    EXPRESS = "express"
    SAME_DAY = "same_day"

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
General patterns

  • Use CamelCase and suffix with Error or Warning: ValidationError, ConnectionTimeoutError, DeprecationWarning
  • Custom exceptions should inherit from a built-in exception class or from your project's base exception: class APIError(Exception):
  • Create a project-wide base exception so callers can catch all your exceptions with one statement: class PaymentError(Exception):

Useful tips

  • For large packages, build an exception hierarchy: DatabaseError → DatabaseConnectionError, DatabaseQueryError, DatabaseMigrationError
  • Name exceptions after the condition they represent, not the action that failed: PaymentDeclinedError (not PayFailedError)
  • Document in the docstring which exceptions a function can raise
  • Use Exception subclasses for recoverable errors; use Warning subclasses for non-fatal issues

General anti-patterns

  • Generic names without suffix: class MyError: (unclear if it's an exception or a data class)
  • Inheriting directly from BaseException (reserved for system-exiting exceptions like KeyboardInterrupt)
  • Exception names that describe the operation instead of the failure: ProcessPayment (sounds like a function)
  • Overly broad names that clash with stdlib: class TimeoutError: (shadows built-in TimeoutError)
# Payment module exception hierarchy
class PaymentError(Exception):
    """Base exception for all payment-related errors."""

class TransactionDeclinedError(PaymentError):
    """Payment was declined by the gateway."""

class InsufficientFundsError(PaymentError):
    """Customer account has insufficient funds."""

class GatewayTimeoutError(PaymentError):
    """Payment gateway did not respond in time."""

class ExpiredCardError(PaymentError):
    """Card is past its expiration date."""

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
General patterns

  • Use snake_case in function names ONLY. Don't look at some bad examples, even if they have 1k+ stars on GitHub
  • Functions which validate or check something and return boolean should start with is_, has_: has_tax_applied(), is_valid()
  • Functions not covered by the above rule should have executable names: compile(), collect(), process(), fetch()
  • If the function has and in the name, there is a high chance it does multiple things. Split it.
  • Name CRUD functions after the resource and action: create_order(), list_customer_orders(), update_shipping_address(), delete_expired_carts()
  • Name query functions by what they return: list_pending_payments(), find_user_by_email(), search_products(), list_active_discounts()
  • Name action functions by the side effect: apply_discount_to(), refund_payment(), cancel_subscription(), dispatch_order()
  • Use domain vocabulary consistently — if you say fetch throughout, never mix in retrieve or get for the same operation
# E-commerce function naming in practice
def calculate_order_total(order_id: int) -> Decimal:
    ...

def apply_promo_discount(order: Order, code: str) -> Order:
    ...

def send_order_confirmation_email(user_email: str, order: Order) -> bool:
    ...

def is_product_in_stock(sku: str) -> bool:
    ...

def refund_line_item(transaction_id: str, amount: Decimal) -> RefundReceipt:
    ...

Useful tips

  • Good function arguments can help to shorten the function name: add_car_to_catalog(name: str) → add_car_to(catalog: Catalog)
  • Pick one verb per operation and never mix. If the codebase uses fetch_ for remote reads, use fetch_ for all remote reads — no retrieve_.
  • Use the module name to shorten function names: 
    # Before
from food import create_french_fries

create_french_fries()
...

# After
from food import france

france.create_fries()
...

# Or even shorter
from food.france import create_fries

create_fries()
...

General anti-patterns

  • Abbreviations: compile_frst()
  • One-letter functions: v()

docs.title: Verb families
docs.text: Choose one verb per operation and keep it in the whole code base. The tables group the verbs by the job they do. For the word order inside a name, see Action and context. For more verbs, see the Glossary below and the master glossary.

docs.title: Query
docs.text:
Verb Use it when Examples get You read data from memory or by a cheap lookup. It raises an error if the item is missing, unlike dict.get. get_order, get_user_email, get_order_total (a stored value) find You return one item by key or criteria, or None. No result is a normal answer. find_user_by_email, find_product_by_sku, find_open_cart list You return a collection, often filtered or paged. list_open_orders, list_active_discounts, list_user_addresses fetch You read over a network or from a slow API. fetch_exchange_rates, fetch_carrier_tracking, fetch_customer_profile load You read stored data from a file or a database into memory. load_cart, load_pricing_rules, load_tax_table search You return many matches, possibly ranked, as a list. search_products, search_orders_by_note count You return the number of matches. count_open_orders, count_unread_notices

One rule decides between the read verbs: get for memory or a cheap lookup, load for local storage, fetch for a network or a slow API. Do not use get_ and fetch_ for the same operation.

docs.title: Command
docs.text: Verb Use it when Examples create You make a new record. create_order, create_refund, create_shipment update You change a record. update_shipping_address, update_cart_item, update_payment_method save You persist a record, new or changed. It pairs with load. save_order, save_cart, save_user delete You remove a record. delete_expired_carts, delete_draft_order, delete_saved_card cancel You stop a planned or running operation. cancel_order, cancel_subscription, cancel_shipment send You cause a message to go out. send_receipt_email, send_shipping_notice, send_payment_reminder apply You put a rule or an effect on data. apply_coupon, apply_tax_rule, apply_shipping_discount refund You give money back. refund_payment, refund_line_item, refund_shipping

docs.title: Boolean
docs.text:
Prefix Use it when Examples is_ You check a state. is_cart_empty, is_order_paid, is_in_stock has_ You check ownership. has_discount, has_saved_card, has_open_order can_ You check ability or permission. can_cancel_order, can_refund_payment, can_ship_express should_ You check a decision. should_retry_payment, should_send_receipt must_ You check a requirement. must_validate_address, must_accept_terms

For all boolean prefixes, including was_, will_ and allows_, see Booleans, collections, units and time.

docs.title: Conversion
docs.text: Pattern Use it when Examples <source>_to_<target> You convert one shape to another. order_to_invoice, cents_to_decimal, cart_to_order to_<target> A method converts its own object. order.to_dict, money.to_decimal, address.to_label from_<source> A class method builds an object. Order.from_cart, Money.from_cents, Address.from_dict parse_<thing> You read text into a structure. parse_coupon_code, parse_delivery_date, parse_price format_<thing> You write a structure as text. format_price, format_address, format_tracking_number serialize / deserialize You convert to and from a transfer format. serialize_order, deserialize_order

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text: Verb Use it when Examples open / close You acquire and release a resource, as a pair. open_session, close_session, open_connection start / stop You run a process. start_worker, stop_worker, start_scheduler pause / resume A process continues later. pause_subscription, resume_subscription initialize You set up state before first use. setup overlaps, so keep one of the two. initialize_cart, initialize_gateway reset You return to the initial state. reset_cart, reset_retry_count dispose You free what an object owns, with no matching open. Where there is an open, use close. dispose_connection_pool, dispose_temp_files

docs.title: Event handler
docs.text: Pattern Use it when Examples on_<owner>_<event> The callback for one named event. on_order_created, on_payment_failed, on_cart_expired handle_<source> An entry point receives a raw message, such as a webhook or a queue message, and calls the on_ functions. handle_payment_webhook, handle_refund_message emit_<event> You publish an event. emit_order_created, emit_payment_captured subscribe_to_<topic> You register for events. subscribe_to_orders, subscribe_to_refunds

docs.title: Validation
docs.text: Verb Use it when Examples validate You read the input and return or raise a list of problems. It never changes state. validate_order, validate_address, validate_coupon verify You confirm that a claim is genuine and raise if it is not. A boolean form is is_signature_valid. verify_signature, verify_email_token, verify_webhook_secret ensure You raise on the first failure of a condition that must hold. It does not repair anything. ensure_cart_has_items, ensure_stock_available check You run a test and return a report or an outcome, not a bare boolean. check_fraud_risk, check_address_deliverability sanitize You remove unsafe content. sanitize_order_note, sanitize_search_query

docs.title: Calculation
docs.text: Verb Use it when Examples calculate You compute a value from inputs. Prefer calculate_ to compute_. calculate_order_total, calculate_cart_tax, calculate_shipping_cost estimate The result is approximate. estimate_delivery_date, estimate_shipping_weight sum You add numbers. It is a narrow case of calculate. sum_line_item_cents, sum_refunds round You change precision. round_to_cents, round_price_up convert You change a currency with a rate. For other units, use the _to_ form: grams_to_ounces. convert_currency, convert_price_to_eur

docs.title: Name by return type
docs.text: Returns Pattern Examples bool is_, has_, can_, should_, must_ is_cart_empty, has_discount One item that must exist get_<item> get_order, get_customer One item or None find_<item> find_coupon, find_user_by_email A list list_<items>, search_<items> list_open_orders, search_products A number count_<items>, calculate_<value> count_open_orders, calculate_order_total A new object create_<thing> (stored), build_<thing> (in memory only) create_order, build_invoice Nothing a verb for the side effect cancel_order, send_receipt_email An iterator iter_<items> iter_order_rows, iter_pending_refunds A converted value <source>_to_<target>, parse_, format_ order_to_invoice, parse_price

docs.title: Bad → better
docs.text:
Bad Better Why order_cancel() cancel_order() Verb first reads as a command. check_stock(sku) returning a boolean is_in_stock(sku) A boolean function uses is_, has_, can_ or should_. do_checkout() (if it completes the checkout) complete_checkout() do adds no meaning. get_and_save_user() get_user() and save_user() and often hides two jobs. get_coupon() that may return None find_coupon() find says that no result is a normal answer. get_all_orders() that returns a list list_orders() list states the return shape. fetch_total() that adds numbers locally calculate_order_total() fetch suggests a remote read. validate_order() that saves validate_order() and save_order() A check must not change state. handle_data(order) (if it applies a coupon) apply_coupon(order) Bare handle_ names no action. process() (if it captures a payment) capture_payment() process hides the action. bare convert(order) (if it builds an invoice) order_to_invoice(order) Name both the source and the target. email(order) (if it sends an email) send_order_email(order) email could be a noun or a verb.

See also

  • Variables for the values these functions take and return
  • Class methods for methods on objects
  • Bad → better cookbook for more rewrites
  • Symmetry for matching pairs such as open and close

docs.title: Modules and packages
docs.text:
General patterns

  • Use snake_case for module (file) names
  • Packages (directories) should be short, lowercase, and avoid underscores when possible
  • Module names should be short, all lowercase, and use underscores only if it improves readability: message_parser.py, http_client.py
  • __init__.py should be empty or only contain package metadata / public API re-exports

Useful tips

  • Name modules after their primary content: a module containing validators → validators.py
  • If a module would shadow a stdlib package, use a compound name: custom_json.py instead of json.py
  • Keep module names under 30 characters to avoid filesystem portability issues
  • Use _ prefix for internal sub-modules: _helpers.py, _types.py

General anti-patterns

  • Dashes in module names (my-module.py — can't be imported with import)
  • Names starting with digits (1_parser.py)
  • Naming a module after a single class inside it — name the module for the category instead: senders.py not EmailSender.py
  • Overly generic names: utils.py, helpers.py (become dumping grounds)
# Well-structured package with consistent naming
payment/
    __init__.py          # re-exports public API
    gateway.py           # payment gateway integrations
    validators.py        # card number, expiry, CVV validators
    _types.py            # internal type aliases, not part of public API
    exceptions.py        # PaymentError, GatewayTimeoutError, etc.

docs.title: Generators
docs.text:
General patterns

  • Prefer a noun or noun phrase when the generator yields objects of a known type: def active_users(): yields user objects
  • Use the iter_ prefix when the generator provides iteration over something: iter_pages(), iter_chunks()
  • Use the generate_ or yield_ prefix when the creation process is the focus: generate_report(), yield_batches()

Useful tips

  • Name generators so the caller intuitively knows to iterate: def unprocessed_orders(): → for order in unprocessed_orders():
  • If a generator wraps another iterator, use wrap_ or prefix the wrapped name: def wrap_lines(file_path):

General anti-patterns

  • Verb-only names that sound like a function with side effects: process() (does it return a generator? modify state?)
  • Using Generator in the name: def user_generator(): → prefer def users():
def unprocessed_orders() -> Generator[Order, None, None]:
    for order in OrderRepository.find_all(status="pending"):
        yield order

def iter_pages(cursor: str | None = None) -> Iterator[list[Record]]:
    while cursor:
        page = fetch_page(cursor)
        yield page.items
        cursor = page.next_cursor

docs.title: Async functions and coroutines
docs.text:
General patterns

  • Prefix network I/O coroutines with fetch_, read_, download_, listen_, poll_
  • Prefix data-processing coroutines with process_, transform_, aggregate_
  • When both sync and async versions exist, name them identically and let the import distinguish them

Useful tips

  • Avoid adding an async_ prefix — the async def keyword already signals the function is a coroutine
  • For long-running coroutines that produce a stream of values, use async for semantics and name as a noun: def event_stream():

General anti-patterns

  • Redundant prefixes: async def async_fetch_data(): → async def fetch_data(): is enough
  • Blocking I/O inside a coroutine without documenting it
async def fetch_order_summary(order_id: str) -> OrderSummary:
    data = await api_client.get(f"/orders/{order_id}")
    return OrderSummary.parse(data)

async def poll_payment_status(transaction_id: str) -> PaymentStatus:
    while True:
        status = await gateway.check(transaction_id)
        if status in (PaymentStatus.COMPLETED, PaymentStatus.FAILED):
            return status
        await asyncio.sleep(2)

docs.title: Decorators
docs.text:
General patterns

  • Use lowercase names, often adjectives or past participles: @lru_cache, @dataclass, @retry, @logged, @deprecated
  • If the decorator takes arguments, name it as a verb or prepositional phrase: @timeout(5), @rate_limit("10/min")

Useful tips

  • Name the decorator for the behavior it adds, not the implementation mechanism: @logged (not @with_logger)
  • Use functools.wraps to preserve the wrapped function's name and docstring
  • For decorator factories, prefer a descriptive name that includes the parameter hint: @retry(tries=3)

General anti-patterns

  • CamelCase in decorators — they are functions, not classes: @RetryOnFailure → @retry_on_failure
  • Naming a decorator after its implementation detail: @wraps_logger instead of @logged
@retry(tries=3, delay=0.5)
@rate_limit(max_calls=10, per=60)
@logged
def process_payment(order_id: str) -> PaymentResult:
    ...

docs.title: Context managers
docs.text:
General patterns

  • Name context managers after the resource they manage: open_file(), database_session(), lock()
  • If the context manager is a class, use CamelCase and a noun: class TemporaryDirectory:, class Timeout:

Useful tips

  • Use @contextlib.contextmanager to turn a single-yield generator into a context manager without writing a class
  • Name context managers so with reads naturally: with database_session(): or with temporary_file():

General anti-patterns

  • Names that describe the setup/teardown mechanism: class ContextManagerForDB: → database_session()
  • Skipping a docstring — context managers have invisible __enter__/__exit__ behavior that must be documented
from contextlib import contextmanager

@contextmanager
def database_session():
    session = Session()
    try:
        yield session
        session.commit()
    except Exception:
        session.rollback()
        raise
    finally:
        session.close()

@contextmanager
def temporary_file(suffix: str = ".tmp"):
    path = Path(f"/tmp/{uuid4()}{suffix}")
    try:
        yield path
    finally:
        path.unlink(missing_ok=True)

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Pytest is the de-facto standard for Python tests. These conventions apply to test files, functions, fixtures, classes, and mocks.

docs.title: Test functions
docs.text:
General patterns

  • Use the test_<unit>_<condition>_<expected> pattern: test_calculate_total_for_empty_cart_returns_zero()
  • Every test name should describe one specific behavior or outcome
  • Name tests so a failing name tells you what broke without reading the body
def test_apply_discount_reduces_total() -> None:
    ...

def test_apply_discount_negative_amount_raises_error() -> None:
    ...

Useful tips

  • One assertion per test when possible. Two assertions about the same result are fine; two about different behaviors suggest a split
  • Avoid and in test names — the same rule as production functions: test_order_cancels_and_refunds() → two tests

General anti-patterns

  • Test names like test_functionality() or test_1() — they explain nothing
  • Tests named after the implementation instead of the behavior: test_calls_apply_method() breaks on refactor

docs.title: Parametrized tests
docs.text:
General patterns

  • Use descriptive id values with pytest.param so failures pin-point the exact case
  • Name the test test_<unit>_<condition>_<expected> and let the param id carry the variation
@pytest.mark.parametrize("email,expected", [
    pytest.param("user@example.com", True, id="valid_standard"),
    pytest.param("user@", False, id="invalid_missing_domain"),
    pytest.param("", False, id="invalid_empty_string"),
])
def test_is_valid_email(email: str, expected: bool) -> None:
    ...

Useful tips

  • Group param ids by scenario: valid_*, invalid_*, edge_* — they sort well in test output
  • Keep the test function body short — if logic is needed, extract a helper

docs.title: Test classes
docs.text:
General patterns

  • Group tests into a class when they share a common fixture or setup: class TestOrderCheckout:
  • Use CamelCase prefixed with Test: TestPaymentGateway, TestDiscountEngine
  • Name the class after the feature or unit under test, not the test runner

Useful tips

  • Use Test prefix so pytest discovers the class automatically
  • Avoid __init__ in test classes — use setup_method or fixtures instead

General anti-patterns

  • Adding Test prefix to non-test classes — they will be collected and attempted as tests
  • Putting every test in one class — group by feature, not by file

docs.title: Mocks and patches
docs.text:
General patterns

  • Name mocks after the object they replace: mock_payment_gateway, mock_email_service
  • Use mock_ prefix consistently for all unittest.mock objects
  • Keep the mock name in the test function signature aligned with the patched target
def test_send_welcome_email_sends_to_user_address(
    mock_email_service: MagicMock,
    sample_user: User,
) -> None:
    result = send_welcome_email(sample_user)
    mock_email_service.send.assert_called_once_with(sample_user.email)

Useful tips

  • Use spy_ prefix for spies (mocks that wrap the real object): spy_logger, spy_cache
  • Use patch() as a decorator when the mock is used by every test in the class; use with patch() when only one path needs it
  • Align mock method names with the real API — if the real method is send(), use mock.send not mock.deliver

General anti-patterns

  • Generic mock names: mock_obj, m — they obscure what is being replaced
  • Mixing mock_ and other prefixes within the same test file
  • Mocking what you don't own (stdlib, third-party libs in integration tests) — prefer integration patching

docs.title: Pytest Fixtures
docs.text:
General patterns

  • Use nouns for fixtures returning final objects: user, order, cart
  • Use verbs for fixtures returning callables: make_user(), build_order(), generate_token()
  • Name fixture files after their domain: conftest.py for session-scoped, order_fixtures.py for domain-specific
@pytest.fixture
def sample_user() -> User:
    return User(email="test@example.com", name="Test User")

@pytest.fixture
def make_user() -> Callable[..., User]:
    def _make_user(**overrides: Any) -> User:
        defaults = {"email": "test@example.com", "name": "Test User"}
        return User(**{**defaults, **overrides})
    return _make_user

Useful tips

  • Name factory fixtures (fixtures that return a function) with a verb so the caller knows to call them: make_, build_, create_
  • Use conftest.py for fixtures shared across multiple test files
  • Add type hints to fixture return values — IDEs and type checkers can then infer types in test functions

General anti-patterns

  • Fixture names that don't reflect the returned object: fixture_user, user_fixture — just user is enough
  • Over-scoping fixtures to session when function is sufficient — it hides test pollution

docs.title: Test name patterns
docs.text:
A test name is a short sentence about one behaviour. The pattern is test_<unit>_<condition>_<expected>. The condition or the expected part may be left out when it is obvious. The examples use an e-commerce checkout.

Part Question Example Unit What is under test? apply_coupon, cancel_order, Cart Condition In which situation? with_expired_code, for_empty_cart, when_card_is_declined Expected What happens? raises_error, returns_zero, refunds_payment

docs.title: Examples by situation
docs.text: Situation Pattern Examples Normal result test_<unit>_returns_<value> test_calculate_total_returns_sum_of_line_items, test_find_user_for_unknown_email_returns_none Edge case test_<unit>_<condition>_<expected> test_calculate_total_for_empty_cart_returns_zero, test_apply_coupon_with_expired_code_raises_error Side effect test_<unit>_<effect> test_cancel_order_refunds_payment, test_checkout_sends_receipt_email State change test_<unit>_sets_<state> test_pay_order_sets_status_to_paid, test_cancel_order_sets_cancelled_at Rule test_<rule>_<outcome> test_free_shipping_applies_above_threshold, test_discount_never_exceeds_order_total Failure test_<unit>_fails_when_<cause> test_checkout_fails_when_card_is_declined, test_refund_fails_when_already_refunded Permission test_<actor>_can_<action> or test_<actor>_cannot_<action> test_customer_can_cancel_unshipped_order, test_guest_cannot_view_other_orders

docs.title: Behaviour, not implementation
docs.text: Tests the implementation Tests the behaviour Why test_calls_apply_method test_apply_coupon_reduces_total The first name breaks on a refactor. The second does not. test_uses_dict_for_cart test_cart_keeps_items_in_insertion_order The reader cares about the result, not the data structure. test_save_called_once test_cancel_order_persists_new_status A call count is a means. The stored state is the goal. test_loop_over_items test_calculate_total_adds_all_line_items A loop is a detail. test_private_helper_returns_true test_checkout_accepts_valid_card Test through the public interface.

docs.title: Test classes and files
docs.text: Kind Rule Examples Test file test_<module>.py, mirrors the module under test. test_order_checkout.py, test_coupon_rules.py Test class Test<Unit> or Test<Feature>. No __init__, because pytest does not collect a class that has one. TestOrderCheckout, TestCouponRules, TestCartMerge Scenario class One class per scenario when the setup is shared. TestCheckoutWithDeclinedCard, TestCheckoutAsGuest Test method Same as a test function. The class names the feature. The method names the rule under test. TestCart.test_add_item_increases_item_count

docs.title: Fixtures and factories
docs.text: Kind Rule Examples Plain fixture A noun for the object it returns. order, cart, customer Fixture in a state A state word and a noun. paid_order, empty_cart, guest_customer Factory fixture A verb for the function it returns. Use create_ if the factory stores the object, build_ if it stays in memory, and make_ if neither applies. make_order, build_cart, create_customer Test data factory A class named for the model, in a factories module. This is the accepted use of the Factory suffix for test data, for example with factory_boy. See Classes. OrderFactory, CustomerFactory Mock fixture mock_ and the replaced object. Use spy_ for a spy. mock_payment_gateway, mock_email_service, spy_logger Session resource A noun for the shared resource. database, http_client, redis_connection Autouse fixture A verb that states the effect. It runs for every test without being requested (autouse=True). freeze_clock, reset_cache, disable_network

docs.title: Bad → better
docs.text:
Bad Better Why test_1 test_cancel_order_refunds_payment A number explains nothing. test_order test_create_order_rejects_empty_cart One behaviour per name. test_happy_path test_checkout_succeeds_with_valid_card Name the case, not the mood. test_error test_checkout_fails_when_card_is_declined The reader sees the cause and the result. test_it_works test_apply_coupon_reduces_total works is not a check. test_calculate_total_and_tax test_calculate_total_adds_line_items and test_calculate_tax_uses_region_rate and hides two behaviours. test_cart_1, test_cart_2 test_cart_merge_keeps_both_items Use the rule instead of a counter. user_fixture user The decorator already marks the fixture. fixture_order order The decorator already marks the fixture. order (a paid order) paid_order Name the state. get_order (a factory fixture) make_order get suggests a read. class OrderTests class TestOrderCheckout The Test prefix is needed by pytest's default discovery.

See also

  • Functions for production function names
  • Classes for production class names
  • Bad → better cookbook for more rewrites
  • pytest: conventions for Python test discovery for the rules about test_ names

docs.title: Advanced test topics
docs.text: The tables below extend the sections above. The examples use an e-commerce checkout.

docs.title: Parametrized ids
docs.text:
An id is the label of one case in the test report. Write the id as a short phrase about the case.

Kind Pattern Examples Valid case valid_<case> valid_standard_email, valid_plus_alias, valid_long_domain Invalid case invalid_<reason> invalid_missing_domain, invalid_empty_string, invalid_double_at Edge case edge_<case> edge_zero_quantity, edge_max_quantity, edge_single_cent Business case <role>_<situation> guest_with_coupon, member_free_shipping, vip_double_points Generated ids pytest.param(case, id=case.name) or a list in ids= when the data is large pytest.param(case, id=case.name) 
@pytest.mark.parametrize("quantity,expected_cents", [
    pytest.param(0, 0, id="edge_zero_quantity"),
    pytest.param(1, 1999, id="valid_single_item"),
    pytest.param(10, 18990, id="valid_bulk_discount"),
])
def test_calculate_line_total_for_quantity_returns_expected_cents(quantity: int, expected_cents: int) -> None:
    ...

docs.title: Mocks, spies and fakes
docs.text:
Kind Rule Examples Mock mock_ and the replaced object. mock_payment_gateway, mock_email_service Spy spy_ and the wrapped object. The real code still runs. spy_logger, spy_cache Fake fake_ and the replaced object. A hand-written working light version, not a unittest.mock object. fake_clock, fake_inventory, fake_payment_gateway Stub stub_ and the replaced object. A hand-written double that returns fixed answers, not a unittest.mock object. stub_tax_rates, stub_carrier_quotes Patch target Patch where the name is used, not where it is defined. patch("checkout.service.send_email") Mock call Assert calls only at an outbound boundary, such as email or a gateway. Assert state elsewhere. mock_email_service.send.assert_called_once_with(user.email)

Use autospec=True or create_autospec so the mock keeps the real signature. For example, create_autospec(PaymentGateway, instance=True) raises AttributeError for charge if the real class has no charge. The prefixes mock_, spy_, fake_ and stub_ are all allowed in one file. Each double uses the prefix of its own kind.

docs.title: Exception tests
docs.text:
Pattern Examples test_<unit>_<condition>_raises_<error> test_apply_coupon_with_expired_code_raises_expired_error test_<unit>_rejects_<input> test_create_order_rejects_empty_cart test_<unit>_fails_when_<cause> (the same as the "Failure" row above; use it when the error type does not matter) test_checkout_fails_when_card_is_declined test_<unit>_<condition>_returns_<result> (for a case that must not raise) test_refund_for_zero_amount_returns_zero_refund 
def test_apply_coupon_with_expired_code_raises_expired_error(expired_coupon: Coupon) -> None:
    with pytest.raises(CouponExpiredError, match="expired"):
        apply_coupon(expired_coupon)

docs.title: Async tests
docs.text:
Kind Rule Examples Test function The same name as a sync test. Add async def. async def test_capture_payment_returns_receipt Async fixture The same name as a sync fixture. No async_ prefix. http_client, database_connection Marker Use the marker or the mode of your async plugin. @pytest.mark.asyncio with pytest-asyncio in strict mode, @pytest.mark.anyio with anyio, no marker in pytest-asyncio auto mode Timing Name the timeout condition, not the sleep value. test_poll_order_status_stops_after_timeout

An async test needs a plugin, such as pytest-asyncio or anyio. Without a plugin, pytest does not run the coroutine. In pytest-asyncio strict mode, an async fixture needs @pytest_asyncio.fixture.

docs.title: Performance and slow tests
docs.text:
Kind Rule Examples Benchmark (measures, never fails) test_<unit>_benchmark, with the benchmark fixture of pytest-benchmark. test_calculate_total_benchmark Limit test (asserts) A measurable limit in the name. Enforce it with pytest-timeout or a benchmark threshold. test_search_products_finishes_within_100_ms_for_10k_items Marker A marker for slow tests. @pytest.mark.slow, @pytest.mark.integration Limits in the name The name must match an enforced limit, for example @pytest.mark.timeout(2). Change both together. test_checkout_finishes_within_2_seconds

Register custom markers in pytest.ini or pyproject.toml and run with --strict-markers, so that a typo in a marker name is an error.

docs.title: Snapshot tests
docs.text:
Kind Rule Examples Test name State the scenario. Use matches_snapshot only when the snapshot is the point of the test. test_order_with_two_items_serializes_to_expected_json, test_invoice_pdf_matches_snapshot Snapshot name Use the test name, or give a short name with the snapshot plugin. snapshot(name="invoice_with_discount"), snapshot(name="order_with_two_items")

A snapshot name should describe the scenario. With syrupy, the snapshot is stored in __snapshots__/<module>.ambr, keyed by the test name, and by <test name>.<name> when you pass name=. Review each snapshot change as a code change. Update snapshots with --snapshot-update.

docs.title: Advanced bad → better
docs.text:
Bad Better Why id="case1" id="invalid_missing_domain" The report shows the reason. mock mock_payment_gateway A bare mock hides the replaced object. patch("payment.gateway.charge") in a test of checkout patch("checkout.service.charge") Patch the name where the code under test uses it. This holds when checkout.service does from payment.gateway import charge. If it calls payment.gateway.charge(...) through the module, patch payment.gateway.charge. test_exception test_apply_coupon_with_expired_code_raises_expired_error The name shows the error and the cause. async def test_async async def test_capture_payment_returns_receipt The test states the behaviour. The keyword async already says that it is async. test_speed test_checkout_finishes_within_2_seconds The limit is in the name. Enforce it, for example with pytest-timeout. test_snapshot_1 test_order_with_two_items_serializes_to_expected_json A counter says nothing. slow_test_checkout test_checkout_end_to_end with @pytest.mark.slow Use a marker, not a prefix. pytest finds tests by test_.

See also

  • pytest: parametrize for ids
  • unittest.mock: where to patch for patch targets
  • pytest: custom markers for markers

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
General patterns

  • Booleans should start with is_, has_, should_: has_completed, is_ready, should_retry
  • Use plural nouns for collections: users = [], pending_orders_by_id = {}, active_sessions = set()
  • Include metric units in the name: delay_seconds, velocity_meters, timeout_ms, buffer_size_kb
  • Use _count and _index for counters: retry_count, page_index. Use _total_<unit> for sums: order_total_cents
  • Use previous_ / next_ for paired state variables: previous_cursor, next_cursor
  • Use new_ / old_ for before-and-after comparison: new_email, old_email
  • Type-annotate all variables, especially when the type is not obvious from the value
  • Name negative booleans as the positive condition to avoid double negatives: is_empty not is_not_empty
# Well-named variables in an e-commerce checkout
customer: Customer = fetch_customer(session_id)
is_cart_empty: bool = cart.item_count == 0
available_discounts: list[Discount] = discount_service.list_active()
selected_shipping_method: ShippingMethod | None = None
total_weight_grams: int = sum(item.weight_g for item in cart.items)
retry_attempts_remaining: int = 3

Useful tips

  • Use i, j, k as loop counters — this is the only acceptable exception to the one-letter rule and only inside tight loop scopes
  • For short-lived scope variables, name the value by its meaning: parsed_order, serialized_payload
  • In list/dict comprehensions, prefer descriptive names for the iteration variable: (user for user in users if user.is_active) not (x for x in xs if x.is_active)
  • Use _ as a throwaway variable name when the value is intentionally unused: _, status = result
  • Align variable names with the domain language from the spec or product requirements

General anti-patterns

  • Abbreviations: dstr = 100.12
  • One-letter variables outside tight loops: v = 'comis'
  • Generic names like data, info, tmp, thing, obj — they convey zero intent
  • Negative boolean names: is_not_empty, has_no_error (forces mental double-negation)
  • Hungarian notation: strName, intCount, dictUsers (type info in a typed language is noise)
  • Redundant prefixes: my_variable, the_value, local_var (adds length, adds nothing)
  • Shadowing built-in names: list, str, id — they look valid but silently break the corresponding function

docs.title: Examples by kind
docs.text: The tables below show one naming pattern for each kind of variable. The examples use an e-commerce checkout. For the rules behind them, see Booleans, collections, units and time and Negation and optionality.

docs.title: Booleans
docs.text: Kind Pattern Examples State (use the positive form) is_<state> is_paid, is_cart_empty, is_active (not is_not_inactive) Ownership has_<thing> has_discount, has_gift_wrap, has_saved_card Ability can_<action> can_cancel, can_refund, can_ship_express Decision should_<action> should_retry, should_send_receipt, should_notify_customer Requirement must_<action> must_verify_email, must_accept_terms Past fact was_<participle> was_refunded, was_restocked Switch is_<feature>_enabled is_express_shipping_enabled, is_logging_enabled

docs.title: Collections, mappings and counts
docs.text: Kind Pattern Examples List plural noun orders, line_items, pending_refunds Set plural noun, or unique_<items> unique_skus, active_sessions Mapping <value>_by_<key> orders_by_id, quantity_by_sku, prices_by_currency Count <thing>_count order_count, retry_count, failed_payment_count Ids <thing>_ids order_ids, coupon_ids Batch <thing>_batch order_batch, refund_batch Index <thing>_index item_index, page_index, row_index

docs.title: Units, time and money
docs.text: Kind Pattern Examples Duration <thing>_<unit> timeout_seconds, retry_delay_ms, session_ttl_seconds Size <thing>_<unit> file_size_bytes, package_weight_grams, buffer_size_kb Timestamp <event>_at paid_at, shipped_at, expires_at Date <event>_on or <thing>_date delivered_on, birth_date Money <owner>_<value>_cents plus currency_code order_total_cents, tax_cents, currency_code Ratio <thing>_rate discount_rate, tax_rate, error_rate

docs.title: Optional, comparison, accumulator and cursor
docs.text: Kind Pattern Examples Optional the plain name, with X \| None selected_shipping_method: ShippingMethod \| None, coupon_code: str \| None Before and after old_ and new_ old_email, new_email, old_quantity, new_quantity Neighbours previous_ and next_ previous_page, next_page Accumulator running_<thing> or <owner>_total_<value> running_total_cents, order_total_cents, packed_item_count Cursor <thing>_cursor order_cursor, next_page_cursor Loop item singular of the collection for order in orders, for line_item in line_items

docs.title: Bad → better
docs.text:
Bad Better Why paid_flag is_paid flag says the type, not the meaning. orders_list orders The plural already says that it is a collection. order_dict (keyed by id) orders_by_id by_id states the key. The type is not in the name. num_items item_count num could mean "number" or "numeric". i (an item index outside a tight loop) item_index A one-letter name is fine only in a tight loop. timeout = 30 timeout_seconds = 30 The unit is in the name. price = 19.99 price_cents = 1999 plus currency_code Integer money avoids rounding errors. _cents fits currencies with 100 minor units only. Otherwise use _minor_units. created created_at _at marks a timestamp. Use created_at_utc when the zone is not obvious. ttl = 3600 ttl_seconds = 3600 A unit removes the guess. discount = 0.2 (a ratio) discount_rate = 0.2 A ratio needs a clear word. coupon = "" (a code string) coupon_code: str \| None = None Absence is not an empty string. prev (a pagination cursor) previous_cursor Spell out the word and name the thing. emails (one address) email A plural name for one value misleads. data (if it holds an order summary) order_summary data fits any variable. disable_cache = False is_cache_enabled = True A negative name with False is a double negative. list = get_orders() orders = get_orders() list shadows the built-in.

Notes

  • X | None needs Python 3.10 or later. Before that, use Optional[X].
  • Omit the unit when the type carries it: a timedelta named timeout, not timeout_seconds.

See also

  • Functions for functions that return these values
  • Bad → better cookbook for more rewrites
  • Glossary for verbs, nouns and suffixes

docs.title: Systems
docs.text:
General patterns

  • Name what crosses a system border with care. A name in an API, an event or a command line is a contract. Callers depend on it
  • Use one style inside one interface. Do not mix snake_case and camelCase in one API
  • Use the same word for the same thing in every interface: customer_id in the REST path, in the event and in the database
  • Follow the standard of the interface when one exists: AIP for HTTP APIs, CloudEvents for events, OpenTelemetry for telemetry, POSIX and GNU for command lines

Useful tips

  • A rename in a language is a refactor. A rename in an API is a breaking change. Choose the name before the first release
  • Write the naming rules of the interface in its style guide, and check them with a linter (for example api-linter for AIP rules or spectral for OpenAPI)
  • Keep a glossary of domain words. The references and glossary page is a start

General anti-patterns

  • Names that leak the implementation: /getOrderFromDb, OrderEntity
  • Names that change by endpoint: userId in one response and user_id in another
  • A verb in a resource path when a standard method fits: /v1/createOrder
